chunks.title: Editorial Header
chunks.text: Editorial Header. The home screen opens with a large serif headline that rotates through a shuffled pool of dictate calls-to-action ("What do you want to dictate today?", "Talk faster than you type. Start here.", "Speak it straight into your last app.", and similar) in place of the former static "Recents." title, with today's date retained as a subtitle directly above the search bar and transcript list. The rotating line doubles as the home's quiet micro-messaging surface, gently coaching the speak-don't-type habit without an extra banner. The top row of the header carries only the circular brand logo (clipped from the app icon art) on the left — the "Jot" text wordmark was dropped, and the logo is sized to read at the same diameter as the Help and Settings glass buttons on the right so the three sit on one line. Cumulative dictation stats — typing time saved today, lifetime dictation count, and a 14-day sparkline — are surfaced in Settings → About rather than on the home page, keeping the home surface focused on recent activity.

chunks.title: Transcript Library with Time Grouping
chunks.text: Transcript Library with Time Grouping. All past recordings are presented in a scrollable list automatically bucketed into four recency groups — Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days, and Earlier — so users can find recent notes without searching. Library entries include transcripts captured from any surface — the main app, the keyboard, Shortcuts, and the Apple Watch app — all interleaved by capture time. Each row shows the recording's timestamp, its duration when known (live dictations record it; file transcriptions via Shortcuts do not), and a two-line excerpt of the transcript text. A note whose automatic cleanup is still running in the background shows a small "Cleaning up" spinner where the rewrite sparkle will appear; when the cleaned text lands, the excerpt and the sparkle fade in rather than snapping. The most recent entry is rendered as a featured one-line serif-italic quote on a soft blue-tinted card at the top of the list, so the newest transcript reads as the headline of the page; the recency label that introduces it (e.g. "Today") sits inside the same blue-tinted panel so the header and featured quote read as a single editorial section. Entries below the featured row, and all other recency sections, use the standard row treatment on the parent card surface. A small coral sparkles glyph appears alongside the timestamp on any row whose transcript has an AI Rewrite — a quiet, glanceable affordance that distinguishes rewritten entries from raw originals. The same coral sparkle appears on the keyboard Recents strip for visual parity. A few voice captures never land in the library by design — for example a Voice Prompt rewrite instruction is used once and never saved as a transcript.

chunks.title: Live Search
chunks.text: Live Search. A persistent search bar at the top of the library filters the transcript list in real time as the user types, matching against both the displayed (cleaned/rewritten) text and the original raw transcript text, so any recording can be located by a remembered phrase regardless of which version it appears in. Every note is also indexed for iOS Spotlight — a search from the Home Screen finds it, and tapping the result opens the note in Jot. Meaning-based search across notes lives in Ask Jot.

chunks.title: Home Empty State
chunks.text: Home Empty State. When the library contains no transcripts, a dedicated empty state is shown in place of the list, inviting the user to make their first dictation.

chunks.title: Home No-Search-Results State
chunks.text: Home No-Search-Results State. When a search query is active but no transcripts match, a "No matches" message is shown with a suggestion to try a different search term.

chunks.title: Floating Dictate Button
chunks.text:
Floating Dictate Button. A prominent blue floating action button labeled "Dictate" sits anchored at the bottom of the home screen. Tapping it navigates to the full-screen Recording Hero via a navigation push.

While a recording is in progress and the user has backed out of the recording surface, the Dictate button is replaced in place by a blue gradient "Recording" pill containing a pulsing white dot, the live elapsed timer, and a small upward arrow. Tapping the pill returns to the live recording surface; the pill carries a soft outer blue wash so it reads as live without dominating the home view.

chunks.title: Transcript Row Actions
chunks.text: Transcript Row Actions. Each transcript row supports a swipe-left gesture that reveals two actions — a red Delete for single-row removal and a Select action that enters multi-select mode with that row pre-selected — so multi-select is discoverable from the swipe rather than hidden. A long-press also enters multi-select (a secondary path) starting with the long-pressed row pre-selected. A short tap on a row opens the Transcript Detail view. Delete triggers a confirmation dialog before permanently removing the entry.

chunks.title: Help Access
chunks.text: Help Access. A question-mark button in the home header opens the Help screen as a modal sheet, accessible at any time without leaving the library.

chunks.title: Settings Access
chunks.text: Settings Access. A gear icon in the home header opens Settings as a modal sheet. It replaces the former profile-avatar circle — a gear reads plainly as "settings" without implying a user account, which Jot does not have.

chunks.title: Multi-Select & Combine
chunks.text: Multi-Select & Combine. Multi-select mode is primarily discoverable from the swipe-left gesture on any transcript row, which reveals a Select action alongside Delete (see §1.7); tapping Select enters multi-select with that row pre-selected. A long-press on a row is kept as a secondary entry path (and the VoiceOver "Enter selection mode" action), also entering multi-select with the pressed row pre-selected. In this mode the Dictate button is replaced by a bottom toolbar with three actions: Select All (selects every visible transcript), Combine (merges 2 or more selected entries into one new transcript, no upper limit), and Delete N (removes all selected entries after a confirmation dialog). Tapping additional rows toggles their selection. Exit multi-select by completing an action or by tapping outside the selected rows. Combine is enabled once at least 2 rows are selected, with no upper limit on how many can be combined. Tapping Combine opens a confirmation dialog with two options: Combine and delete originals (destructive — the source entries are removed and replaced by the new combined one) and Combine and keep originals (the new combined entry is created alongside the originals). In both cases, the combined entry is built from the best available version of each source — if a source has an AI Rewrite, the rewrite is used; if it does not, the original transcript is used. The picked strings are joined oldest-first (the earliest dictation appears at the top of the combined entry, the most recent at the bottom) with paragraph breaks. This is the opposite of the library's visual order — the library shows newest on top — because the combined entry reads naturally as a chronological narrative rather than as a stack of the rows in display order. The result is stored as the new entry's original (the new combined entry has no Rewrite of its own and no Rewrite tab). The new entry receives a fresh timestamp and ledger number.

chunks.title: Ask Jot Entry Point
chunks.text: Ask Jot Entry Point. A small sparkles pill sits next to the search bar in the home header. Where search finds a remembered phrase, this opens Ask Jot — natural-language Q&A across all the user's notes. The pill appears only where Ask can run — iOS 27 on an iPhone with Apple Intelligence (see §14.6) — so the entry point is never shown in a non-working state.

chunks.title: Light & Dark Appearance
chunks.text: Light & Dark Appearance. The entire app follows the system Light / Dark setting automatically — the page wallpaper, Liquid-Glass cards, editorial type, and every text color shift to their dark variants over a near-black page, with no in-app appearance switch. The Jot Keyboard and Apple Watch app follow the same system appearance (the watch is always on a true-black backdrop). Brand, status, and semantic-icon colors stay constant across both modes; only surfaces, text inks, and keyboard chrome adapt.

chunks.title: Full-Screen Recording Surface
chunks.text:
Full-Screen Recording Surface. The app presents a dedicated full-screen recording view primarily in three cases: the user taps the home Dictate button; the user taps Dictate on the Jot Keyboard from another app with no Warm Hold active (a *cold* start — the surface opens with a "head back to your app" coaching cue); or the user re-enters a recording they had backgrounded, via the home "Recording" return pill. Dictation that stays in context never shows this surface: keyboard dictation while Jot is already foreground and voice-editing inside a transcript both record inline into the focused field, and the Action Button Shortcut and Warm-Hold keyboard dictation record in the background without presenting it.

Exception — keyboard dictation within the Warm Hold window: when a warm-hold session is still active, tapping Dictate in the keyboard does NOT bring Jot to the foreground. The recording starts in the background and the user remains in the host app; only the keyboard's streaming strip animates to reflect recording state. See §2.9 and §13.2 for details.

chunks.title: Recording Status Indicator
chunks.text: Recording Status Indicator. Recording state is communicated implicitly — the dedicated full-screen surface and the live streaming transcript make it unmistakable that the microphone is active. The elapsed-time counter lives inside the blue stop button at the bottom of the screen as a monospace timer, so the duration of the session is always visible alongside the primary "stop" affordance rather than as a separate top-of-screen status line. During the external-keyboard cold-start withhold window (§2.1's exception case), the freed top space above the transcript carries quiet rotating micro-messages (e.g. "Recording stays on while you go," "looking away helps you find the words," "the thinking happens out loud, not on the screen"). Once the live stream reveals, or on an ordinary FAB-initiated recording, the freed top space instead shows a single fixed caption above the transcript ("A sharper transcriber takes a second pass when you stop and tidies the live text."), not a rotating pool.

chunks.title: Live Streaming Transcript
chunks.text: Live Streaming Transcript. While the user speaks, a scrolling text area displays a continuously updating live preview of what is being said, rendered in an italic serif font. The preview is produced by the active dictation engine: Apple's engine (the default) streams it natively and firms it up in place as you talk, as does Jot's own engine for English; for Jot's other languages it is refreshed by re-reading the most recent stretch of audio in sentence-sized chunks at natural pauses and every few seconds. Either way it is a rough running approximation, not the final text (see §2.8). The view auto-scrolls to follow the newest text so the user always sees the most recent words without manually scrolling. A soft fade at the top edge signals that more content exists above. Because the preview arrives in sentence-sized chunks (at speech pauses or every few seconds), the newest visible words can trail the voice by a few seconds — a quiet ellipsis sits right after the last word, its dots brightening in a slow cycle, signaling that transcription is still catching up and more text is on the way. With Reduce Motion enabled the ellipsis is a steady static one, and it disappears entirely while paused since nothing is being captured. The same trailing ellipsis appears in the keyboard's streaming strip. This live preview can be turned off with the "Live text while dictating" toggle in Settings → Dictation (on by default; turning it off saves battery and does not change the saved transcript; off by default on lower-memory iPhones) — the saved final transcript is unaffected (§2.8).

chunks.title: Pause / Resume
chunks.text: Pause / Resume. A Pause control sits on the recording surface alongside Stop and Cancel. Pausing temporarily stops capturing audio without finalizing the recording — the session stays live and the same dictation continues when the user resumes, so the paused gap is simply absent from the saved audio. While paused, the recording dot goes static/hollow and the surface reads "Paused · mic ready, not capturing," and the elapsed timer freezes (it counts only time actually captured, so it resumes from where it left off). The microphone is kept warm during the pause for instant resume, which is why iOS keeps showing its orange microphone indicator — but nothing is captured or stored while paused, exactly as during Warm Hold; the on-screen wording makes the held-but-not-recording state explicit. The live streaming preview is preserved across a pause and new words append after resume rather than restarting. Only Resume or Stop / Cancel leave the paused state; a forgotten pause auto-finalizes once the session reaches the overall recording cap. Pause/Resume is available from both the recording surface and the Jot Keyboard.

chunks.title: Stop and Finalize
chunks.text: Stop and Finalize. A large blue gradient stop button at the bottom of the screen ends the recording. The button contains a white stop square and the running elapsed-time monospace counter side-by-side. After stopping, the live text holds still on screen and the caption above it becomes a stage line with a stepping ellipsis — "Finishing the transcript…", then "Cleaning up with “Cleanup”…" (naming whichever prompt runs) while Automatic Cleanup with AI runs, or "Applying your follow-up…" for a chained command — and the stop button shows a spinner with the matching one-word stage ("Transcribing", "Cleaning up", "Rewriting"; never a generic "Working", and never flashing back to "Transcribing" in the last moments) while the on-device speech model produces the final accurate transcript from the audio captured during the session — which may differ from the live preview shown during recording. The Cancel control dims once Stop is tapped: the take is finished and on its way to the library. Stop ends the recording from either the active or a paused state.

chunks.title: Cancel Recording
chunks.text: Cancel Recording. A circular red trash-icon button at the trailing end of the bottom control row (alongside Pause/Resume and Stop) discards the current recording without saving any transcript, useful when the user dictated the wrong thing or changed their mind. It discards from either the active or a paused state; once Stop has been tapped it dims and does nothing, because the recording is complete and being saved (§2.5).

chunks.title: Backgrounding the Recording Surface
chunks.text: Backgrounding the Recording Surface. The recording surface includes a visible back chevron at the top-left. Tapping it backgrounds the recording without cancelling it — for example, to glance at the home screen or another app — and the standard iOS edge-swipe-back gesture works the same way in parallel. The microphone and live transcription keep running; the home surface replaces the Dictate button with a blue "Recording" return pill that taps back into the live recording surface. When that backgrounded recording is stopped (from the keyboard, the Live Activity or Siri), the pill stays in place in a quiet finishing form — a small spinner and the stage word, "Transcribing" or "Cleaning up", with no timer and nothing to tap — until the note lands in the list; only then does the Dictate button return. Stopping or cancelling are the only ways to actually end a recording (see §2.5 and §2.6).

chunks.title: Live Preview & Final Transcript
chunks.text: Live Preview & Final Transcript. How the live preview relates to the final saved transcript depends on the dictation engine. With Apple's engine (the default), the live preview streams natively as the user speaks and firms up in place; when the user stops, the transcript is finalized right away, so stopping stays fast even after a long dictation. With Jot's own engine, it depends on the language. English streams the live preview as the user speaks and has the transcript already written by the time they stop, so stopping is instant however long the dictation ran — that is the more accurate English model that downloads itself in the background; until it has landed, English behaves like the other languages below. For every other language, a single accurate model does both passes — there is no separate "fast" streaming model: while the user speaks it produces the live preview by repeatedly re-reading a trailing window of the recent audio (in sentence-sized chunks, at natural pauses and every few seconds), and when the user stops it re-reads the entire recording once more for the clean, fully-punctuated final. Either way the saved transcript can differ from — and reads better than — what scrolled by live, and it is always the version saved to the library. The live preview is the one part that can be switched off — via the "Live text while dictating" toggle in Settings → Dictation (and off by default on lower-memory iPhones) — without affecting the saved final transcript. On a fresh install or just after an update, Jot's own engine may still be loading for the first dictation; recording still begins the instant the user taps and nothing said is lost while it loads (see §2.14 and §2.9).

chunks.title: Auto-Dismiss on Completion
chunks.text:
Auto-Dismiss on Completion. Once transcription finishes, the recording view dismisses itself automatically and the user lands on Jot's home view, with the new transcript already saved and available in the library.

When the dictation was initiated from a third-party app's keyboard (via the Jot down key) and there is no active Warm Hold session (cold start), Jot is brought to the foreground during recording and the user must manually swipe back to the host app — for example, by swiping right along the iOS app-switcher gesture bar. The transcribed text is pasted into the originating text field once the user returns to that app. Jot does not automatically switch the user back to the host app. On a fresh install or right after an update, the on-device speech model may still be loading when this cold start fires; in that case the recording begins capturing the instant the user taps — their voice is buffered while the model finishes loading, so nothing said during the wait is lost — and, only if the load is genuinely slow, the surface shows a short reassuring cold-start line (no progress bar) until the model is ready and the transcript catches up. Stopping before the model has finished simply waits for it, then transcribes the buffered audio.

Within the Warm Hold window, this flow is different: Jot is never brought to the foreground, so no manual swipe-back is needed. The keyboard's streaming strip shows recording progress in place, and when transcription completes the text is auto-pasted without the user leaving the host app. See §13.2 for the Warm Hold UI-path disclosure.

chunks.title: Automatic Clipboard Copy on Completion
chunks.text: Automatic Clipboard Copy on Completion. When an in-app dictation — started from the home screen Dictate button or Recording Hero — finishes and the final transcript is saved, Jot automatically places the automatically cleaned transcript text on the system clipboard. The user can immediately paste it into any other app (Notes, Messages, Mail, a browser field, and so on) without any extra step: no need to open the transcript detail, tap a copy button, or long-press the row. This auto-copy happens as soon as the transcription completes — at the same moment the result becomes available to the Jot Keyboard — and precedes the Auto-Dismiss that returns the user to the library. The Action Button Shortcut similarly copies its result to the clipboard on completion; both flows share this behavior. Manual copy options — the row long-press, detail Copy button, and Actions Pane "Copy last" — remain available for later retrieval of any transcript.

chunks.title: Chained Follow-Up Voice Commands
chunks.text:
Chained Follow-Up Voice Commands. Within 30 seconds after a dictation completes, the user can make a short follow-up dictation to transform the prior text — for example, "make it shorter" or "translate that to Spanish." Jot recognises this as a command against the just-dictated text rather than a new separate dictation: the transformed result replaces the prior text on the clipboard, a new transcript entry is created, and the original no longer appears in the keyboard's recent history. Outside the 30-second window, all new dictations are treated as fresh independent entries.

In the new entry's detail view, the command utterance itself (e.g., "make it shorter") becomes the Original tab text, while the transformed prior dictation appears under the Rewrite tab. This means a user opening the follow-up entry sees their voice command as the Original and the rewritten text — attributed as "Rewritten with [model name]" — as the Rewrite.

Home library vs. keyboard recents asymmetry: in the Home library, both the original transcript and the follow-up entry appear as separate rows — the original is not hidden or marked in any way. In the keyboard's recents strip, only the follow-up entry is shown; the original is filtered out and does not appear. A user browsing the Home library therefore sees the full chain, while a user glancing at the keyboard recents sees only the latest result.

See also: keyboard chained follow-up cross-reference.

chunks.title: Accessibility: VoiceOver Focus
chunks.text: Accessibility: VoiceOver Focus. When the recording surface opens via an automated entry path — such as a keyboard-initiated recording triggered by a deep link — VoiceOver focus is placed on the recording status element (pulsing dot and elapsed timer) so assistive technology users are immediately informed that recording is underway, rather than landing on the back-navigation button.

chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation
chunks.text:
Apple Watch Dictation. Jot ships a standalone Apple Watch app (watchOS 26+) for capturing thoughts directly from the watch — useful when reaching for the phone is awkward. Recording works without the iPhone present: audio is captured locally on the watch as a small compressed file and queued. Whenever the watch comes within range of the paired iPhone running Jot, queued recordings transfer automatically in the background and run through the same on-device transcription pipeline as in-app dictations — the resulting transcript appears in the Home library alongside everything else. The watch app is introduced to new users on the final Setup Wizard completion panel (W8), which surfaces a "one more thing" Apple Watch card.

Watch home screen. The screen opens directly on a large round blue "dictate" button that glows and slowly breathes — no app-name title, since you're already in the watch app. Tapping it starts recording; "Tap to dictate" sits just below. The page then scrolls into a "Recent" section: a header row with an "All N" link to the full list (shown once there are more than three transcripts), then any recordings still waiting on the phone shown at the top as "Waiting to sync" cards (a play button, the status, and how long ago it was captured in amber) — each disappears the moment the phone confirms receipt, with the finished transcript following seconds later. Tap a "Waiting to sync" card to play the recording back on the watch speaker (useful to hear, or to recover, one that's stuck), or swipe it left to delete it if you don't want to sync it. Below the pending cards sit the three most recent transcripts as tap-to-open cards. Recordings sync automatically, so there is no top-of-screen pending badge or success ribbon. At the very bottom — only reachable by scrolling past the transcripts — a single muted "Sync diagnostics ›" footer row leads to the connection-status surface and Reset sync button.

Recording sheet.

chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation
chunks.text:
Below the pending cards sit the three most recent transcripts as tap-to-open cards. Recordings sync automatically, so there is no top-of-screen pending badge or success ribbon. At the very bottom — only reachable by scrolling past the transcripts — a single muted "Sync diagnostics ›" footer row leads to the connection-status surface and Reset sync button.

Recording sheet. Modal sheet centered on a large round coral button with the running mm:ss timer inside it — tapping the button stops and saves. The button carries no "Stop" word; a quiet "Tap to stop" hint sits below a live coral amplitude waveform. The button + waveform freeze (waveform replaced by a static "REC" cue) in Always-On Display and when Reduce Motion is enabled. The only outcome is a saved recording — there is no discard path: even dismissing the sheet saves the capture rather than losing it, so accidental taps can't lose audio. Recordings cap at 15 minutes per session; the watch warns at 14:30 with a haptic and banner so long captures aren't silently truncated. An extended runtime session keeps the recorder alive while the wrist is lowered.

Recent transcript list. The watch surfaces the most recent ten transcripts (read-only — taps open a full-text view; all editing happens on the phone). The top three appear inlined on the home screen as individual cards; the rest are one tap away via "All N". Watch-originated entries show a small watch glyph next to the date; transcripts captured on the phone show no glyph (the absence is the default). Recordings still waiting on the phone appear as "Waiting to sync" cards at the top of both lists — tap one to play it back, swipe left to delete it — and each clears as soon as the phone has it, with the real transcript following moments later. Opening a transcript shows its full text plus a "Synced to iPhone" confirmation row. A "Last synced" footer surfaces in amber on the full list if it's been more than 24 hours since the last successful sync.

Dictation language on the watch.

chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation
chunks.text:
Recordings still waiting on the phone appear as "Waiting to sync" cards at the top of both lists — tap one to play it back, swipe left to delete it — and each clears as soon as the phone has it, with the real transcript following moments later. Opening a transcript shows its full text plus a "Synced to iPhone" confirmation row. A "Last synced" footer surfaces in amber on the full list if it's been more than 24 hours since the last successful sync.

Dictation language on the watch. Before recording, the user can scroll the Digital Crown to pick the dictation language from the same list available in Settings → Dictation → Language. The choice travels to the iPhone automatically, so when the queued recording is transcribed it uses the language selected on the watch — no separate step on the iPhone is needed. Most languages use Apple's on-device dictation on the iPhone and need nothing extra; the European languages only Jot's own engine can do require that iPhone to have already downloaded the one-time multilingual model (see §4.8 and §6.1). Like phone-captured dictations, a watch recording's source audio is retained on the iPhone for 3 days once it syncs, so it can be re-transcribed in another language within that window.

Complications + Smart Stack tile. A watch complication (corner, circular, inline variants) and a Smart Stack tile let the user start a recording in one tap from any watch face — both deep-link straight into the recording sheet.

Storage cap. The watch holds at most 50 pending recordings before new captures are blocked with an explicit alert ("Watch storage full — open Jot on iPhone to sync"). Fail-closed by design: silently dropping the oldest unsynced recording would be worse than the brief friction of forcing a sync.

chunks.title: Cold-Start Loading
chunks.text: Cold-Start Loading. When a dictation starts while the speech model is still loading — typically the first dictation after an install or update, or after the system reclaimed the model's cache — recording begins capturing the instant the user taps (§2.9), so nothing said is lost. On a fast/warm load nothing special is shown beyond the normal "Listening…". Only a genuinely slow cold load surfaces a short reassuring line, and during a long load that line rotates through a few different messages so it doesn't sit static — there is no progress bar, no percentage, and no model name. This applies on both the recording surface and the keyboard streaming strip; the live transcript replaces it the moment the model is ready.

chunks.title: Dictation Engine
chunks.text: Dictation Engine. Jot transcribes with Apple's on-device dictation by default, for every language Apple supports on the device — English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin (in Simplified and Traditional script picks), and Cantonese. Spanish is offered as two picks — Spanish (European) and a separate Spanish (Latin America) — because the two are recognized best by different regional models; Latin-American Spanish always uses Apple's engine (with Mexican-Spanish recognition), since Jot's own engine only has European Spanish. Cantonese is likewise offered as two picks — Cantonese (Hong Kong) and Cantonese (Mainland China) — recognized by Apple's two regional Cantonese models. It runs entirely on the iPhone or iPad, streams the live preview natively as you speak (see §2.8), and — because it's Apple's own engine — works on more devices: newer hardware uses Apple's newer, higher-accuracy dictation, and hardware too old for that automatically uses Apple's older but broadly-compatible dictation, so on-device dictation still works on devices where Jot's own engine can't run. Jot's own on-device engine (the more accurate one, historically Jot's only engine) is offered as an optional upgrade on the devices that can run it — iPhone 14 Pro and later, and iPad with M1 or later — through a one-time keyboard nudge that invites the user to switch to it for more precise dictation, keeping Apple's engine as a fallback. For English, Jot's own engine uses a newer, more accurate English model that punctuates as it transcribes, streams the live preview natively, and finishes the transcript the instant the user stops (§2.8); it downloads itself once in the background over Wi-Fi (§6.1), and until it arrives — or if it can't be fetched — English is transcribed by the built-in model that ships with the app, with no interruption either way. The nudge only appears for a language Jot's own engine can actually run — never the CJK languages or Latin-American Spanish, which stay on Apple.

chunks.title: Dictation Engine
chunks.text: For English, Jot's own engine uses a newer, more accurate English model that punctuates as it transcribes, streams the live preview natively, and finishes the transcript the instant the user stops (§2.8); it downloads itself once in the background over Wi-Fi (§6.1), and until it arrives — or if it can't be fetched — English is transcribed by the built-in model that ships with the app, with no interruption either way. The nudge only appears for a language Jot's own engine can actually run — never the CJK languages or Latin-American Spanish, which stay on Apple. Anyone who was already using Jot before Apple's engine became the default keeps Jot's own engine after updating — the switch to an Apple default only changes what a brand-new install starts on. Jot's own engine is also the only engine for the European languages Apple can't do (Polish, Czech, Ukrainian, and others — see the Language picker), which download a one-time multilingual model. On devices that can't run Jot's own engine, Apple's dictation is simply used with no engine choice to make. Your custom vocabulary is applied on either engine (except for Japanese, Korean, Mandarin — Simplified or Traditional — and Cantonese, which Apple transcribes without the vocabulary pass). The engine choice is invisible in normal use — the recording surface and keyboard look and behave the same either way.

chunks.title: Original / Rewrite Tabs
chunks.text: Original / Rewrite Tabs. The detail view for any transcript presents two tabs — Original and Rewrite — selectable via a two-pill segment control. The Original tab always shows the unmodified text produced by the speech model. The Rewrite tab shows the automatic cleanup output when present, and later shows the output of AI Rewrite if one has been generated; older entries with neither show an empty state with a prompt to create one. When cleanup or a rewrite already exists, the detail view defaults to the Rewrite tab on open so the improved text is immediately visible. While an automatic cleanup is still running for the note, a small "Cleaning up…" card sits above the text until it lands. A third Speakers tab appears alongside these two only when a multi-voice recording has been split into speaker turns — otherwise the segment control stays a two-pill (or single-tab) control.

chunks.title: Transcript Metadata
chunks.text: Transcript Metadata. A subline at the top of the detail view displays the relative recording date and the duration when available (present for live dictations; omitted for file transcriptions via Shortcuts), giving context without cluttering the reading area. A small language label appears in this subline alongside the existing provenance glyphs (such as the watch glyph for Apple Watch–originated entries) to indicate the language the transcript was dictated in — useful at a glance when the library contains notes in multiple languages. This recorded language is also used as the source for the Translate action and determines which language is offered for re-transcription. The detail view has no title surface — title and tag fields are intentionally absent from v1 (see also §7.11).

chunks.title: Selectable Text
chunks.text: Selectable Text. Both the original transcript text and the rewrite text are fully selectable, allowing users to copy any portion to the clipboard using the standard iOS text selection handles. On devices with Apple Intelligence, selecting the text also surfaces the system Writing Tools (Rewrite, Make Concise, Proofread, and more) — that is iOS's own selection menu, available on any selectable text. Jot's own Rewrite runs the user's prompts itself and never asks the user to go through that menu (§7.2).

chunks.title: Rewrite Attribution
chunks.text: Rewrite Attribution. When a rewrite is present, a small attribution line says how it was made: "Cleaned up automatically with “Cleanup”" for a rewrite produced by Automatic Cleanup with AI (naming whichever prompt ran), or "Rewritten with “<prompt name>”" for one the user ran from the note — followed by how long ago it landed. Notes rewritten before this attribution existed fall back to naming the engine, Apple Intelligence (§7.2). The attribution row also hosts the rewrite feedback affordance (thumbs up / thumbs down) and the Discard rewrite button.

chunks.title: Rewrite Feedback
chunks.text: Rewrite Feedback. The Rewrite Attribution row hosts a 👍 / 👎 pair to the left of the Discard button. Tapping one sets the rating; tapping the active glyph again clears it; tapping the opposite glyph swaps it. A light haptic confirms each tap and the glyph fills in (hand.thumbsup.fill in accent blue or hand.thumbsdown.fill in red) when active. The rating is local and private; nothing is uploaded. It pairs with the Edit Rewrite flow to produce a complete signal — a 👎 plus a user correction is the strongest data for future model fine-tuning, but each half is meaningful on its own (a 👎 with no edit still says "this was wrong but I didn't have time"; a 👍 with no edit says "the model nailed it"). The rating clears whenever the underlying rewrite changes — tapping Rewrite regenerates the rewrite and resets the rating; Discard clears the rewrite, edit, and rating together (see §13.5).

chunks.title: Action Bar
chunks.text: Action Bar. A row of actions at the bottom of the detail view provides five actions, left-to-right: Delete, Edit, a Rewrite control (an accent sparkle circle that opens the rewrite Prompt Picker), a Translate globe (opens the on-device Translate sheet for the active tab directly), and Copy. The earlier full-width "Rewrite" pill was replaced by the compact sparkle circle so it no longer dominates the bar. Delete sits on the far-left so the destructive action is harder to hit accidentally; Copy sits on the far-right where the right-hand thumb naturally falls. The Copy button is icon-only — there is no visible text label. After tapping Copy, the icon changes to a checkmark briefly before reverting to the copy icon after approximately 1.3 seconds, confirming the action to the user. The VoiceOver accessibility label updates from "Copy transcript" to "Copied to clipboard" during this window. Tapping Delete shows a confirmation dialog before the entry is permanently removed. When the entry has no AI Rewrite, it reads "Delete this entry?" with a destructive "Delete" button and a "Cancel" button. When a rewrite exists, it instead reads "Delete this entry or just the rewrite?" with three options: "Delete this entry" (destructive), "Delete rewrite only" (destructive, discards just the rewrite and keeps the original), and "Cancel".

chunks.title: Rewrite Progress and Cancellation
chunks.text: Rewrite Progress and Cancellation. When a rewrite is actively running, a progress card appears alongside the action bar (the action bar itself remains visible) with a "Rewriting…" indicator and a Cancel button, allowing the user to abort the generation mid-stream.

chunks.title: Edit Transcript
chunks.text: Edit Transcript. The Edit pencil in the action bar turns the currently-visible tab into an editable text field with a slim bottom bar offering Cancel and a blue Save (✓) button. The tab pill is hidden while editing — one tab at a time. Editing the Original tab overwrites the transcript text in place; the pre-edit speech-model output is not retained (the user's correction becomes the new ground truth). Editing the Rewrite tab keeps the model's rewrite frozen as the "before" and saves the user's correction as the "after," so the pair is preserved as a future-improvement training signal (see §13.5). Tapping Rewrite after an edit generates a fresh rewrite and clears the prior user-edit; tapping the Rewrite tab's Discard affordance clears both the model rewrite and any user edit together. The Edit pill is disabled while a rewrite is mid-flight. Leaving mid-edit is protected rather than blocked: if nothing has been changed, the back chevron and the swipe-back gesture simply leave the editor and go back, but once there are unsaved changes tapping back asks first — “Save your changes?” with Save, Discard Changes, and Keep Editing — and the swipe-back gesture is held off while those changes are pending, so work is never lost to an accidental swipe. While editing, dictating into the field works the same way as any other focused field in Jot: tap Dictate on the system or Jot keyboard, and the transcribed text is inserted at the cursor when the keyboard's recording stops — there is no separate in-editor microphone control. While editing, any text the user adds or changes during this session — whether typed or dictated — is shown in *italic*, while the untouched original text stays upright, so it's easy to see exactly what was changed. The italic is a live editing cue only: on Save everything is stored as plain text and the next time the entry is opened it all reads upright again. Edit mode also offers Find & Replace for fixing a repeatedly-misheard word in one pass.

chunks.title: Edit Transcript
chunks.text: While editing, any text the user adds or changes during this session — whether typed or dictated — is shown in *italic*, while the untouched original text stays upright, so it's easy to see exactly what was changed. The italic is a live editing cue only: on Save everything is stored as plain text and the next time the entry is opened it all reads upright again. Edit mode also offers Find & Replace for fixing a repeatedly-misheard word in one pass. On iOS 27 the edit bar also offers Proofread — a checkmark button that runs the iPhone's own grammar and spelling checker over the draft (no AI model, no quota, works offline). Flagged words are underlined in orange, and a sheet lists each suggestion with the checker's note; the user taps a replacement or Ignore for each one — nothing is ever applied automatically, because dictated names and vocabulary terms are exactly what a checker likes to "fix". Accepting a fix edits the draft in place (italic, like any other session edit) and re-checks; typing clears the underlines until the next Proofread. Whenever Apple Intelligence is available, the edit bar also offers an AI sparkle button ("Rewrite draft with AI" to VoiceOver) that opens the same prompt picker as the transcript's sparkle — your saved prompts, Voice prompt and Translate — and rewrites the current draft in place — on either tab — with the chosen prompt on Apple Intelligence; the center label reads "Rewriting…" while it runs, and the result lands as a session edit (italic, like typed or dictated changes), so Save keeps it and Cancel discards it — nothing reaches the saved note without a Save. Jot no longer selects the text and points at the system Writing Tools menu (§3.3). A rewrite started from the keyboard's recents strip does not open edit mode at all: it runs straight onto the note's Rewrite tab (§7.10).

chunks.title: Translate
chunks.text: Translate. The Rewrite Prompt Picker includes a Translate option that opens a lightweight translate sheet. The source is the transcript’s own recorded language (visible as the language badge in the subline); the user picks a target language from a row of chips — all supported languages including English — with the transcript’s own language excluded from the list. The active tab’s text — whether the Original or the Rewrite — is translated instantly, shown as a serif quote with Copy and Share actions. Translation is read-once: it is not saved to the transcript, does not occupy the Rewrite tab, and leaves both the original and any rewrite untouched. It runs entirely on this iPhone using the system’s built-in translation (offline after a one-time per-language download the system manages), so the text never leaves the device (§13.1). It is distinct from the optional “Translate to…” rewrite-prompt template, which runs through Apple Intelligence and *saves* into the Rewrite tab — this Translate option is faster and ephemeral. Translating here also downloads the language pack the keyboard's own Translate needs. See also §3.11 for the related option to re-run transcription in a different language while the source audio is still retained.

chunks.title: Find & Replace (while editing)
chunks.text: Find & Replace (while editing). While editing a transcript, a magnifying-glass button in the edit bar opens a Find & Replace bar above the keyboard — for when the speech model misheard the same word several times. The user types a word to find (whole-word, case-insensitive matches are counted live) and a replacement, then taps Replace All to fix every occurrence at once; the changed words show in *italic* like any other edit until Save. Find & Replace operates on whichever tab is being edited (Original or Rewrite) and is available only in edit mode. When a replacement looks like a genuine term correction — a one- or two-word term that isn't an everyday word, swapped in two or more places — Save shows a gentle one-tap offer to add the corrected term to your vocabulary: it adds the term and saves the misheard form as a visible "sounds-like" on it, so the next dictation can write the term (the same correction as selecting a word and choosing Add to Vocabulary — see Learn from corrections). When the edit itself already taught that pair (Save learns from edits on its own), the offer isn't shown again. The offer is dismissible and never blocks; declining changes nothing.

chunks.title: Source Audio Retention & Re-Transcribe
chunks.text: Source Audio Retention & Re-Transcribe. Jot keeps the source audio of every recording on-device for 3 days — silently and automatically, and never leaving the device (§13.1). The 3-day window is measured from when the audio enters Jot, not from when it was originally spoken: for a live dictation that is the moment the recording finishes, and for a file shared into Jot from another app it is the moment the import completes — so a shared clip always gets its full 3 days on-device regardless of how old the file was. Within that window, a re-transcribe affordance appears in the transcript detail subline (the same area as the language badge): the user picks a language and Jot re-runs the speech model on the original audio, replacing the transcript text with the new result. This is useful when, for example, a note was dictated in English before the multilingual model was downloaded, and the user wants to switch the transcription to a European language — they download the model (see §6.1 and §4.8), then re-transcribe while the audio is still retained. After 3 days the audio is deleted automatically (no manual step needed) and the re-transcribe affordance disappears; the saved transcript text is unaffected. The retained audio is excluded from iCloud Backup and is stored only locally. Re-transcription produces a new language badge reflecting the chosen language and acts as the new source for Translate. While the audio is still retained, it is also what Detect speakers runs on.

chunks.title: Speaker Notes
chunks.text: Speaker Notes. When a recording has more than one voice, Jot can split its transcript into per-speaker turns. On any transcript whose source audio is still retained, a Detect speakers action lives in the detail overflow menu — the same ⋯ menu as Re-transcribe — and runs an on-device pass that groups the audio by who is talking. If it finds more than one speaker, the detail view gains a third Speakers tab beside Original and Rewrite, listing each turn with its speaker label, its time range, and its text (selectable like the rest of the transcript). Voices are labeled "Speaker 1", "Speaker 2", and so on in the order they first speak. It works on one-mic meetings and calls — voices talking over each other in a single recording — for up to 8 speakers; a stray second of someone else in a solo note doesn't count as a second speaker. Audio shared into Jot from another app (for example a call recording) is checked for multiple speakers automatically right after it is transcribed, so a multi-voice import arrives already carrying its Speakers tab; a single-voice note changes nothing, and speaker detection never blocks, delays, or fails an import — if it can't run, the transcript is saved exactly as it would be otherwise. Because the saved turns hold the transcript text exactly as it read at detection time, editing the Original text or re-transcribing the audio clears the Speakers tab (you can run Detect speakers again while the audio is still retained). Speaker detection runs entirely on this iPhone (§13.1); it uses NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 speaker model (about 190 MB, a one-time download) that Jot fetches quietly over Wi-Fi so it is ready when needed, and downloads on demand otherwise. Running Detect speakers again uses the same model; turns saved by earlier versions stay as they were.

chunks.title: Welcome (W1)
chunks.text: Welcome (W1). The first wizard panel introduces Jot with a large wordmark headline and a short tagline ("Voice transcription for fast messaging — dictate into any app."), followed by a quiet supporting line that states the core value proposition up front — free, private, and fully on-device (your words never leave your iPhone). It then offers a single "Get started" call-to-action that begins the setup flow. W1 also has the standard wizard close (X) button with a "Skip setup?" confirmation prompt (same as on every other panel).

chunks.title: Microphone Permission (W3)
chunks.text: Microphone Permission (W3). The microphone-permission panel requests microphone access via the system permission dialog. If the user grants permission, the wizard advances automatically. If permission was previously denied, the panel shows a deep-link button that opens iOS Settings directly to Jot's permission page so the user can enable it without hunting through menus.

chunks.title: Keyboard Installation & Full Access (W4)
chunks.text: Keyboard Installation & Full Access (W4). The keyboard-installation panel sends users to Keyboard Settings once to add Jot and turn on Full Access. When the keyboard has not been detected, the panel title reads "Add the Jot keyboard" and the primary call-to-action reads "Open Settings"; when the user returns with Jot installed, the title updates to "Keyboard ready" and the button changes to "Continue." Jot can detect keyboard installation via the system's installed-keyboards list, but it cannot detect Full Access directly — Full Access remains a manual user attestation. A secondary "I've already added it" button is shown only in the not-yet-detected state as an escape hatch; once the keyboard is detected, "Continue" is the only footer action. See §13.3.

chunks.title: How It Works (W5)
chunks.text: How It Works (W5). The how-it-works panel is a looping animated mini-phone illustration cycling through four numbered steps — "Tap Jot down on your keyboard," "Jot opens and starts recording," "Swipe back to your app," "Stop from the keyboard when you're done" — each highlighted in sync in a step list below the animation as it plays. An honest footnote above the "Got it" button explains the app-switch: iOS doesn't let keyboards use the mic directly, so Jot hops to the foreground to capture; if that ever changes, the hop goes away. Honors Reduce Motion (the animation freezes on its final frame). This orientation screen has no required user action other than reading and tapping "Got it". This same animated scene is reused on the Help → How Jot Works page.

chunks.title: Keyboard Try-It (W6)
chunks.text: Keyboard Try-It (W6). The keyboard try-it panel is a guided "try the keyboard" step. The user taps a practice field, which raises the keyboard; if the system keyboard appears instead of Jot, an in-field cue tells them to tap the globe key to switch to the Jot keyboard (escalating to "it's the bottom-left key" if they linger). They tap "Jot down", their words stream live in the keyboard, and on stop the result is pasted into the practice field as an "it works" moment, following the normal automatic cleanup path. The user then taps Continue themselves — the panel does not auto-advance — and a manual "I tried it" button allows skipping. By the time the user reaches this panel the speech model is usually ready, so the dictation starts without a wait; on a fresh install where it is still loading, the same cold-start line appears briefly and the result still arrives. This is the wizard's only "try it" step — practicing inside the wizard surface was dropped so users experience Jot exactly as they will use it after setup.

chunks.title: Warm Hold Opt-In (W7)
chunks.text: Warm Hold Opt-In (W7). The warm-hold panel offers the Warm Hold feature: keeping the microphone session alive for 2 minutes after each recording to reduce startup latency for the next dictation. The user flips a "Keep mic ready" toggle (showing an "Always" / "Off" status) and taps Continue; the choice is saved to Settings and can be changed later via Settings → Privacy, where the duration is also customizable (60s, 2 min, 3 min, 5 min, or 30 min).

chunks.title: Completion (W8)
chunks.text: Completion (W8). The eighth and final panel congratulates the user with a "You're ready." headline and a body line ("Jot works now — start dictating in any app, any time."), then closes onboarding with a single "Start jotting." call-to-action. There is no longer a fork to an optional AI Rewrite step — AI Rewrite is set up later from Settings → AI whenever the user wants it, not during onboarding. Below the body, W8 shows a "one more thing" Apple Watch card — a soft-blue tile with a watch glyph, the title "It's on your wrist, too," and a line noting that ideas captured on the watch sync back automatically — introducing the Apple Watch app before the user finishes setup.

chunks.title: Dictation Language Picker (W2)
chunks.text: Dictation Language Picker (W2). The language-selection panel is the second wizard step — it appears immediately after the Welcome screen, before the Microphone Permission step. The list shows only the languages that actually work on this device, and never offers a download that couldn't run here. English is selected by default and needs no download. Many common languages — Spanish (European and a separate Latin-American Spanish), French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese (Hong Kong and Mainland China) — are handled by Apple's on-device dictation and also need no download. Choosing one of the additional European languages that only Jot's own engine can do (Polish, Czech, Ukrainian, and others) triggers a one-time multilingual model download (~632 MB); the panel shows download progress in place and advances to a "Ready" state when complete, unlocking every such language at once so future switches among them cost nothing extra. The searchable language list keeps a Recent section pinned at the top — the active language followed by the ones most recently used (up to five) — so switching among a handful of languages doesn't mean scrolling the full list each time; the recents are shared with the Settings language picker. The selection is saved and can be changed later from Settings → Dictation → Language; on the Apple Watch the Digital Crown serves the same language-selection role. Choosing a language here is the first step toward re-transcribing a note in a different language.

chunks.title: Wizard Navigation Chrome
chunks.text: Wizard Navigation Chrome. Every wizard panel except Welcome (W1) shares a consistent chrome: a back chevron (top-left) that steps to the previous panel, and a close button (top-right, X) that exits the wizard entirely. Welcome has no previous step, so the back chevron is absent on that panel. Tapping the close button shows a "Skip setup?" confirmation dialog before dismissing. If a recording is in progress when the wizard is exited, the recording is stopped automatically so no audio is left capturing in the background. A left-edge swipe gesture (drag rightward from the leading 22 pt strip) performs the same back action as the back chevron.

chunks.title: Wizard Progress Dots
chunks.text: Wizard Progress Dots. At the top of every wizard panel, a row of eight dots represents the eight setup steps. The current step's dot is larger and filled in the accent color; completed steps are smaller filled dots; upcoming steps are smaller outlined dots.

chunks.title: Dictation-Only Design
chunks.text: Dictation-Only Design. Jot's keyboard is dictation-only and has no QWERTY layout. Users keep their regular system keyboard for typing and switch to Jot only to dictate. This is surfaced explicitly in the How It Works wizard step so users understand the intended workflow before completing setup.

chunks.title: Full Custom Keyboard
chunks.text: Full Custom Keyboard. Jot replaces the system keyboard with a fully custom layout when active. The layout is recording-controls-first: a top information strip and an action row with the primary controls — Pause + Stop + Cancel, with Cancel rendered as a trash-can on the left for easy reach — plus a single adaptive Enter key whose glyph adapts to the host field's return action (return-arrow, search glyph, Go, or Send). On wider devices the controls and Enter sit in one line; on narrower devices the layout adapts and keeps Enter on its own row below. The keyboard uses native side margins so it does not span the full screen width, sits at a fixed height, and styles itself to match the host app's light or dark appearance automatically. Below it, Apple's fixed system row (globe / dictation) remains. See §5.4 Dictate / Stop and §5.8 Pause / Resume.

chunks.title: Recents Strip (Idle State)
chunks.text: Recents Strip (Idle State). When the keyboard is idle (not recording), the top strip shows up to ten recent dictation entries with their timestamps and truncated cleaned text. Each row is split into two tappable zones: the body (timestamp + text) re-inserts that transcript at the cursor, and a small trailing Rewrite button (a wand-and-stars glyph, accent color) brings the main app to the foreground, opens that transcript's detail view (§3), and runs the rewrite right away — the Cleanup prompt on Apple Intelligence, landing on the note's Rewrite tab; a note that already has a rewrite simply opens on that tab, and with Apple Intelligence off the note opens the AI settings sheet instead — polishing a dictation from the keyboard is one tap instead of four. (This slot used to be a plain "open in app" arrow; it was replaced because rewriting is what people actually reach for there.) The strip is scrollable, with a soft fade at the bottom edge indicating additional entries below. Entries that have an AI Rewrite display a small coral sparkles glyph inside the body zone before the trailing button — the same affordance used in the home library so the visual language stays consistent across surfaces. A "See all" link brings the main app to the foreground via a deep link. If the app is on the home screen with no overlays active, the transcript library is visible; the deep link does not force a navigation reset, so if a sheet or other navigation is already open the user will not automatically land on the library. Full Access is required for the recents strip to show any content: without it, the entire strip is replaced by an instructional card ("Enable Full Access to Dictate") with a lock-shield icon and the two-step path to turn it on (iPhone Settings → General → Keyboard, then Keyboards → Jot Keyboard → Allow Full Access) (see §5.11).

chunks.title: Recents Strip (Idle State)
chunks.text:
Full Access is required for the recents strip to show any content: without it, the entire strip is replaced by an instructional card ("Enable Full Access to Dictate") with a lock-shield icon and the two-step path to turn it on (iPhone Settings → General → Keyboard, then Keyboards → Jot Keyboard → Allow Full Access) (see §5.11). While a row is held, it lights with a subtle blue highlight and a thin leading accent bar so the user can see exactly which entry their touch is on, and a small contextual hint appears in the strip header naming the action — "Pastes here" while pressing a row body, "Rewrite in Jot" while pressing the trailing button. This is purely visual feedback layered on the existing gestures: a tap still pastes, and pressing then scrolling still scrolls the list without pasting, exactly as before.

### 5.2a Warm-Hold Switching Nudge
After the user has bounced between another app and the keyboard to dictate a few times in a row, the top strip can temporarily show a nudge card in place of the recents strip: "Bouncing back and forth to dictate? Keep the mic ready so the next one starts instantly." with two actions — "Keep mic ready" (turns on Warm Hold) and "Don't show this again" (dismisses the suggestion for good). It only appears for users who haven't already enabled Warm Hold, and never interrupts an in-progress dictation. It takes precedence over its sibling nudges — the engine upgrade and Vocabulary setup — and only one of the three ever shows at a time.

### 5.2b More-Accurate-Engine Upgrade Nudge
On devices that can run Jot's own dictation engine (iPhone 14 Pro and later, iPad M1 and later), after the user has dictated a handful of times on Apple's default engine in a language Jot's own engine can run, the keyboard's top strip can show a one-time nudge card in place of the recents strip: "More accurate dictation available." / "Switch to Jot's own on-device engine." with two actions — Switch (opens a short sheet in the main app that explains Jot's own engine is more precise for English and runs fully on-device, with Apple's engine kept as a fallback) and Not now (dismisses the suggestion for good). What confirming on the sheet does depends on whether Jot's engine is already on the device: if it is, the switch is instant and the sheet confirms "You're on Jot's engine"; if it isn't yet, Jot downloads it in the background over Wi-Fi — usually while the phone charges — no waiting, no cellular data — and switches over automatically once it lands, at which point a brief "You're on Jot's engine" note appears the next time you're on the home screen. While that download is pending, reopening the sheet shows "Downloading… we'll switch you automatically," with a Stop download option that cancels it and keeps Apple. Apple's engine keeps working the whole time. On a device that can't run Jot's engine, when there isn't enough free space, or if the download fails, the sheet says so plainly and keeps Apple's engine (with a Try again on failure) rather than dead-ending.

While that download is pending, reopening the sheet shows "Downloading… we'll switch you automatically," with a Stop download option that cancels it and keeps Apple. Apple's engine keeps working the whole time. On a device that can't run Jot's engine, when there isn't enough free space, or if the download fails, the sheet says so plainly and keeps Apple's engine (with a Try again on failure) rather than dead-ending. It is a twin of the Warm-Hold switching and Vocabulary setup nudges — same card style, never shown at the same time as either, and never interrupting an in-progress dictation. It appears only once; either declining or switching retires it for good. This nudge and its sheet are the user-facing way to move off Apple's default engine (see §2.15).

### 5.2c Vocabulary Setup Nudge
When Vocabulary Boost is still off, the keyboard's top strip can show a one-time nudge card in place of the recents strip: "Get names & jargon spelled right." / "Turn on Vocabulary so Jot learns your words." with two actions — Set up (opens the Vocabulary screen in the main app, where the user can turn the feature on and add their first terms; nothing is ever enabled automatically) and Not now (dismisses the suggestion for good). It appears either when the user has already added custom words but the feature is off (so their words are going unused) or once a regular dictation habit has formed. It is a sibling of the Warm-Hold and engine-upgrade nudges — same card style, and the three are coordinated so only one ever shows at a time (warm-hold first, then vocabulary, then the engine upgrade) with a quiet day between any two, so answering one nudge never leads straight into another. Never interrupts an in-progress dictation; declining retires it for good, and turning Vocabulary on makes it moot.

chunks.title: Streaming Strip (Recording State)
chunks.text: Streaming Strip (Recording State). When a dictation is in progress inside the keyboard, the top strip transforms into a live recording display: a blue pulsing dot, an elapsed timer, a six-bar animated waveform, a brief header status line ("We tidy this up when you stop") noting the live text gets a cleanup pass once recording ends, and a scrollable pane that shows the live preview transcript in real time, rendered in the same small italic serif used by the recording surface. The strip does not vanish when the user stops: it stays through the post-stop wait, holding the last live text still under a header that names the wait (§5.5). This live preview honours the same "Live text while dictating" setting as the recording surface; with it off the pane stays empty and only the final transcript pastes on stop. When a cold start begins before the speech model has finished loading, the pane shows the same cold-start loading treatment in place of the partial text — a short reassuring line (no progress bar) only if the load is genuinely slow — and switches to the live transcript the moment the model is ready (recording is already capturing the whole time, so nothing said during the load is lost). The pane is bottom-anchored — the first words appear near the bottom of the pane and older lines push upward as more text arrives — with the same trailing "still transcribing" ellipsis as the recording surface's live preview (quiet accent-blue dots right after the newest word, brightening in a slow cycle; static under Reduce Motion) and a top-edge fade for overflow; the visible stream is capped to a bounded height so it never grows past the strip. While the dictation is paused, the pulsing dot goes static/hollow, the timer freezes, "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" is shown, and the waveform hides; the partial text already shown is kept (its trailing ellipsis hidden, since nothing is being captured) and resuming appends to it.
