chunks.text: The pane is bottom-anchored — the first words appear near the bottom of the pane and older lines push upward as more text arrives — with the same trailing "still transcribing" ellipsis as the recording surface's live preview (quiet accent-blue dots right after the newest word, brightening in a slow cycle; static under Reduce Motion) and a top-edge fade for overflow; the visible stream is capped to a bounded height so it never grows past the strip. While the dictation is paused, the pulsing dot goes static/hollow, the timer freezes, "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" is shown, and the waveform hides; the partial text already shown is kept (its trailing ellipsis hidden, since nothing is being captured) and resuming appends to it. A "↓ live" pill appears when the user has manually scrolled up and the view is no longer tracking the newest content; tapping the pill restores auto-follow. Follow-up voice commands (see §2.11) apply within the 30-second window after the keyboard dictation completes.

chunks.title: Dictate / Stop Control
chunks.text: Dictate / Stop Control. A prominent pill button in the keyboard's action row toggles recording on and off. The label and appearance change to reflect the current state — "Dictate" when idle, active stop styling when recording — so the current state is always unambiguous. While recording it is joined by Pause / Resume and a trash-can Cancel on the left (§5.1). When Full Access is not enabled, the button displays "Enable Full Access" and tapping it opens Jot's iOS Settings page (from which the user navigates to Keyboards → Jot to toggle Full Access) instead of starting a recording.

chunks.title: Post-Stop "Working" State
chunks.text: Post-Stop "Working" State. Immediately after the user stops a keyboard dictation, the streaming strip stays on screen and goes still — the pulsing dot becomes a static hollow dot, the waveform disappears, the elapsed clock (on wide keyboards) freezes at the recording's length, and the live text is held exactly where it was — while its header line says what the wait is for: "Finishing the transcript" while the speech model finishes on-device, "AI is tidying this before it pastes" while Automatic Cleanup with AI runs (when it is on and set to paste the cleaned-up text), or "Applying your follow-up" for a chained follow-up command. The Jot down button shows a spinner with the matching one-word stage — "Transcribing", "Cleaning up", "Rewriting" — never a generic "Working", and the word does not flash back to "Transcribing" in the last moments before the paste. Once the text is inserted, the strip crossfades back into the recents strip with the new entry on top. If the cleanup couldn't run, the raw words paste and an amber status banner says "Cleanup didn't run — pasted as spoken". If Jot has a candidate correction to the user's custom vocabulary, the keyboard normally holds the paste and shows a small review card asking the user to answer one question (e.g. "what should this say?") before the text is inserted at all — see §8.8 Vocabulary Correction Prompts in the Keyboard. If a candidate correction isn't ready in time (a late-arriving check that lost the race with the paste), it is never asked about after the fact — the pasted text stands, and the suggestion remains reviewable on the transcript in Jot. The only card that ever appears *after* a paste is the one-time split-word teaching card (see §8.8), which never alters pasted text.

chunks.title: Actions Pane
chunks.text: Actions Pane. The ••• actions button opens a full-width actions pane in the keyboard's top region (in place of the recents strip, never overlaying the controls), laid out as a grid of tiles. Selecting text in the host field opens the pane by itself, so Rewrite, Copy and Add to Vocabulary are one tap away; when the selection is cleared, a pane that opened itself closes again, while a pane the user opened with ••• stays open. The pane never opens itself during a live dictation or over a vocabulary review card. Feature tiles (top row): Add to Vocabulary — adds the host's currently-selected word to the Vocabulary term list (enabled only with a selection); Rewrite — with text selected in the host field, rewrites it in place with the user's Cleanup prompt on Apple's on-device model, right there in the keyboard (§7.15); with nothing selected the tile is washed and a tap answers on the tile itself ("Select text"), and with Apple Intelligence off the tile is washed and a tap says "Turn on Apple Intelligence in Settings to rewrite here"; Translate — with text selected, opens a row of language chips and translates the selection in place, on the iPhone (§7.16); with nothing selected the tile is washed and a tap answers on the tile ("Select text"); and Cleanup — the one tile that is a *switch*, turning Automatic Cleanup with AI on or off without opening the app (off by default). Its icon square is purple when on and plain when off, with a small "On" / "Off" chip on the corner; tapping flips it in place with a haptic, and that flip is the whole confirmation — no message (§5.10). When Apple Intelligence can't run the cleanup the off tile is washed and a tap explains ("Turn on Apple Intelligence in Settings to use AI cleanup"); without Full Access the tap says so.

chunks.title: Actions Pane
chunks.text: Its icon square is purple when on and plain when off, with a small "On" / "Off" chip on the corner; tapping flips it in place with a haptic, and that flip is the whole confirmation — no message (§5.10). When Apple Intelligence can't run the cleanup the off tile is washed and a tap explains ("Turn on Apple Intelligence in Settings to use AI cleanup"); without Full Access the tap says so. Edit tiles (bottom row): Copy, Paste, and Undo / Redo — Undo/Redo work off a stack (up to 20 steps) and each shows a count badge of how many steps remain that way; tapping Undo moves one step to the redo side and vice-versa, so the badges always reflect what's available. There is no Close tile: while the pane is open the ••• key becomes an ×, and tapping it closes the pane. The pane never grows a status row, so its tiles always stay fully visible. A tap that can't do anything answers on the tile it hit: the label briefly reads "Select text", "Select a word", "Clipboard empty" or "Nothing to undo" in amber while the tile gives a small shake, then turns back after about two seconds. A longer explanation (Apple Intelligence off, a language not downloaded) closes the pane and appears in the status banner on the Recents card, which is also where rewrite and translate progress and results appear.

chunks.title: Backspace
chunks.text: Backspace. The backspace key deletes one character per tap. There is currently no hold-to-repeat behavior.

chunks.title: Pause / Resume
chunks.text: Pause / Resume. While a keyboard dictation is in progress, a Pause control sits in the action row next to Stop and the trash-can Cancel (§5.1). It is the same Pause / Resume behavior as the recording surface: pausing keeps the microphone warm and the dictation open without finalizing it, the streaming strip shows "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" with a static dot and frozen timer, and resuming continues the same dictation with new words appended. Pause can be initiated and cleared from the keyboard without bringing the main app to the foreground; the paused/resumed state stays in sync between the keyboard and the recording surface.

chunks.title: Dark / Light Mode Adaptation
chunks.text: Dark / Light Mode Adaptation. The keyboard reads the host app's keyboard appearance setting and renders itself accordingly, so Jot's keyboard matches dark-mode apps natively without any user configuration. The rest of the app adapts to the system appearance the same way — see §1.13.

chunks.title: Full Access Requirement
chunks.text:
Full Access Requirement. The return key works without Full Access. Backspace and Undo/Redo also work without Full Access. The following actions are specifically gated:

- Jot down: when Full Access is absent, the Jot down button is replaced by an "Enable Full Access" CTA (with a lock-shield icon). Tapping it opens iOS Settings to Jot's app-settings page; from there the user navigates General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Jot Keyboard → Allow Full Access to flip the toggle.
- Paste: the Paste row in the Actions Pane stays visually enabled and tappable without Full Access (it is never dimmed), but tapping it silently does nothing, because clipboard reads are unavailable. No error is shown.
- Copy: the Copy row in the Actions Pane is silently disabled without Full Access, because the keyboard can only read the host's selected text when Full Access is granted. No error is shown.
- Status banner: the banner that relays dictation result messages is suppressed entirely when Full Access is absent.
- Recents strip content: without Full Access the entire strip is replaced by an instructional card guiding the user to enable it (see §5.2) — there is no "See all" link to tap in this state, since the strip itself isn't shown.

The Setup Wizard guides users through enabling Full Access during initial setup. See also §6.4 Privacy Controls for the Full Access informational row in Settings and §13.3 Full Access Disclosure for the canonical explanation of why Full Access is required.

chunks.title: Auto-Paste of Completed Dictation
chunks.text: Auto-Paste of Completed Dictation. When a keyboard dictation finishes and the transcript is ready, the keyboard automatically inserts the automatically cleaned text into the host app's focused text field — no tap required. This is the core workflow the How It Works wizard step illustrates: speak, stop, and the text appears at the cursor. The auto-paste arms at the moment the user taps Stop and fires as soon as the final transcript is available.

chunks.title: Speech Model Management
chunks.text:
Speech Model Management. Jot chooses the dictation engine and any speech model automatically, based on the language and the device — there is no engine selector or variant picker in normal use. Most languages are transcribed by Apple's on-device dictation, which needs no download and is available immediately on install, so the first dictation works offline. The European languages Apple can't do use Jot's own engine with a separate multilingual model downloaded once on first selection. Jot's own engine is also offered as an optional English accuracy upgrade on capable devices (iPhone 14 Pro and later, iPad M1 and later) through the keyboard nudge — there is no engine toggle to hunt for here. On those same capable devices Jot's own engine transcribes English with a more accurate English model that it fetches for itself: it downloads once in the background over Wi-Fi at a moment the device picks, needs no tap and no permission to proceed, and simply takes over when it is ready. Nothing waits on it — English works from the moment Jot is installed, and switches to the better model silently once it lands (it also brings instant stops and a natively streamed live preview). Because none of this is something the user manages, the Settings card is labelled "Dictation" and carries only two controls — no model name, no readiness pill, no engine picker, and no "runs entirely on this iPhone" footer:

- Language — a picker for the dictation language. It lists only the languages that work on this device and never offers a download that can't run here. English and the other Apple-supported languages are available with no download. A single status line sits under the picker: for English on Jot's own engine it reports the more accurate English model's state — waiting to download, downloading with a percentage, loading, or ready — so it is always possible to tell which model a dictation just used, and it never blocks anything (English is built in and ready throughout).

chunks.title: Speech Model Management
chunks.text:
A single status line sits under the picker: for English on Jot's own engine it reports the more accurate English model's state — waiting to download, downloading with a percentage, loading, or ready — so it is always possible to tell which model a dictation just used, and it never blocks anything (English is built in and ready throughout). Choosing one of the European languages that only Jot's own engine can do triggers a one-time multilingual model download (~632 MB); once downloaded, every such language is unlocked and switching among them is free. The picker menu keeps a Recent section at the top — the active language plus the ones most recently used (up to five, shared with the wizard language picker) — for quick switching without scrolling the full list. The same language choice is made during the first-run Setup Wizard language step. On the Apple Watch, the Digital Crown sets the language on the watch side and the choice syncs to the iPhone. The selected language is recorded with each transcript (visible as a language badge in Transcript Detail) and used as the source for Translate. Any transcript's source audio can be re-transcribed in a different language.
- Live text while dictating — a toggle (on by default) that controls whether the live preview is shown while recording. Turning it off saves battery and does not change the saved transcript; it starts off by default on lower-memory iPhones. One connected effect: the more accurate English model writes the transcript *as you speak*, so with live text off English is transcribed by the built-in model instead (and the larger one isn't downloaded or kept in memory) — everything else about dictation is unchanged.

Vocabulary Boost applies on either engine (except for Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese — see §2.15), regardless of these settings.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Settings Link
chunks.text: Vocabulary Settings Link. A row shows the current count of custom vocabulary terms and navigates to the full Vocabulary settings screen where terms can be managed.

chunks.title: AI Settings Link
chunks.text: AI Settings Link. A row in the AI section shows whether Apple Intelligence is ready for AI Rewrite and navigates to the full AI settings screen. The screen opens with an engine strip that reports Apple Intelligence readiness ("Ready · on your iPhone", or — on iOS 27 when the on-device model is unavailable — "Ready · uses Private Cloud Compute") with a Settings shortcut when it is off (see §7.8). There is one rewrite engine — the user's saved prompts on Apple Intelligence (§7.2) — so there is no engine picker and nothing to download. Below the strip sit the AI cleanup card (§7.14) and the saved-prompt list (§7.7). There is no choice of which model answers Ask Jot — Ask always uses Apple's Private Cloud Compute (see §14.5).

chunks.title: Privacy Controls
chunks.text: Privacy Controls. A Privacy section shows a tappable Full Access row (subline "General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Jot", trailing external-arrow), plus a toggle for Warm Hold after wizard step W7. When Warm Hold is on, the toggle is followed by a "Ready for" duration picker with 60s, 2 min, 3 min, 5 min, and 30 min options. The Full Access row opens iOS Settings to Jot's app-settings page; the subline gives the user the breadcrumb to navigate from there to Allow Full Access (Jot cannot read its state directly — see §13.3). The bottom-of-section caption "Dictation stays on your iPhone. Ask and long rewrites use Apple's Private Cloud Compute — end-to-end encrypted, never stored. No accounts, no telemetry; only feedback you send is ever transmitted." carries the privacy message (see §13.1); no separate "On-device only" row is shown. The matching "Your privacy is protected" explainer is shown on the iOS system-Settings page for Jot, not as a row here (see §13.6a).

chunks.title: About & Support
chunks.text: About & Support. An About section provides links to Help & Support (opens Help), an Apple Watch row (opens a screen showing watch connection status with a Reset sync button — see §2.13), Re-run setup wizard (restarts the Setup Wizard from the beginning for troubleshooting or exploration), Send feedback (opens an in-app feedback form — see §9.6), the app version number, Donations (opens the in-app Donations screen), Jot for Mac (opens the Jot for Mac screen), a Privacy Policy link, an Acknowledgements screen (see §6.6), and a Diagnostics screen — a scrollable on-device log of recent app events (recording start/stop, paste outcomes, the vocabulary gate's decisions, and every failed or deferred AI cleanup or rewrite with its reason, such as the iPhone limiting background AI work) that can be copied or cleared, surfaced for troubleshooting and containing no personal data (relocated here from the Help screen). When at least one dictation has been recorded, a "Time saved" row appears as the first entry of the About card, showing minutes saved today, the cumulative dictation count, and a small 14-day blue sparkline — the same lifetime stats that the home page used to surface inline, relocated here so the home view stays focused on recent activity (see §1.1).

chunks.title: Acknowledgements
chunks.text: Acknowledgements. A dedicated Acknowledgements screen credits the open-source software and open-weight models that Jot is built on. It is organised into two sections: "Models & fonts" — listing the on-device speech models and the typeface used in the app, each with the author, license type, and a tappable link to the upstream source — and "Swift packages" — listing the major third-party Swift packages used by the app, with attribution and source links. Note: the list is curated and may not include every package the app uses. A footer note reiterates that all speech recognition and AI rewriting runs on-device and that no audio or transcript data is shared with any of the credited parties.

chunks.title: Donations
chunks.text:
Donations. The Donations screen is reached from Settings → About as an in-app navigation push. It explains Jot's free model, optionally personalizes the message with the user's estimated time saved when they have dictated for at least five minutes, and shows a searchable list of charities with their current Jot-raised totals. Live totals, donation counts, and the community total come from Jot's donations summary feed; each charity's one-line description (and logo, where available) comes from Jot's charity metadata file and is merged in by charity. Each charity row offers $2 and $10 quick-give actions that open the matching Every.org donation page in the system browser. If current totals cannot be refreshed, the screen shows the last known totals when available, or a retry state when no totals have ever loaded.

A gentle donation prompt also appears on the home screen as a centered popup once the user has built up meaningful usage — gated on cumulative dictation time and a one-week grace after first use so brand-new users are never asked on day one. It re-appears at increasing usage milestones rather than only once: choosing "Not now" simply defers it to the next milestone. The prompt offers "See donations" (opens the in-app Donations screen — the native charities list, not the external website) or "Not now", and never blocks dictation. The usage totals that drive it persist across app updates. The same cumulative usage total also drives the one-time Jot for Mac home prompt, shown in the same popup style.

chunks.title: Your Data (Export & Import)
chunks.text:
Your Data (Export & Import). *Currently hidden behind a flag — not reachable in the shipped app; the feature below is fully built but switched off pending a decision to re-expose it.*

A Your Data area in Settings lets the user export all their transcripts to a file and import them back. Export produces a single file containing every transcript (Original and Rewrite text); the user can save it to Files, share it, or send it anywhere they can keep a file. Import reads such a file and merges the transcripts into the library — the operation is idempotent: re-importing a file that contains entries already on the device never creates duplicates, so it is safe to import the same export more than once. This is an on-device backup and restore safety net for the transcript library, independent of iCloud Backup (see §13.4 for what iCloud Device Backup does and does not include) — it works on devices without iCloud, and the user controls the file. It does not export AI Rewrite prompts, vocabulary terms, or app preferences — only transcript content.

chunks.title: Jot for Mac
chunks.text:
Jot for Mac. A permanent "Jot for Mac" row in Settings → About opens a dedicated screen pitching the Mac app (same on-device dictation, on a bigger screen). The screen shows the download site's address, a "Send to your Mac" button that opens the system share sheet with the download link — the easiest way to hand it to another device, whether that's AirDropping it straight to the Mac or messaging/emailing the link to yourself — and an "Open jot-transcribe.com" button that opens the site directly in Safari.

Separately, a one-time home-screen prompt — "Jot is on your Mac too" — appears once after the user has built up about an hour of cumulative dictation time, in the same centered-popup style as the donation prompt. Unlike the donation prompt it never re-appears: choosing "Get Jot for Mac" or "Not now" both permanently retire it, since there's only one Mac app to point at. "Get Jot for Mac" opens the same Jot for Mac screen described above.

chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup
chunks.text: Automatic Cleanup. Jot strips the most obvious filler tokens — "um", "uh", "er", "uhm", "erm" and their elongated variants — from every dictation before it lands on the clipboard or in the library. This is a fast lexical sweep that always runs: there is no toggle, no separate model, no extra download, and nothing leaves the device. Five other languages get their own hesitation sounds stripped with the same sweep — Spanish ("eh", "em"), French ("euh"), German ("äh", "ähm", "öh", "hm"), Italian ("ehm", "mmm") and Portuguese ("hum"). Each language strips only its own list, never English's, because the English tokens are real words elsewhere ("um" is German for "around", "er" is German for "he"); words that merely *look* like hesitations are never touched either, so Spanish "este" and German "halt" survive. Languages with no hesitation list of their own (Japanese, Polish, Russian, the rest) pass through untouched, and the separate pass that turns spelled-out numbers into digits stays English-only in every case — its rules would misread French "six cents" (600) as a currency amount. In English that pass writes money, percentages, times, dates and years as digits — including the spoken shorthands "one fifty dollars" ($150), "a dollar fifty" ($1.50 at the end of a phrase) and unhyphenated years like "twenty twenty five" or "nineteen eighty four" (2025, 1984), while leaving counting runs ("eighteen nineteen twenty") and phrases like "the twenty eighty rule" as numbers. The cleaned text is what appears in the Original transcript surface, gets pasted into the host app, and is what AI Rewrite operates on when invoked. Paragraph boundaries inserted by the segmenter are preserved (the sweep only consumes adjacent spaces, never newlines), and obvious words containing filler-like substrings ("umbrella", "umpire", etc.) are left intact because the sweep is anchored on word boundaries.

chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup
chunks.text:
The cleaned text is what appears in the Original transcript surface, gets pasted into the host app, and is what AI Rewrite operates on when invoked. Paragraph boundaries inserted by the segmenter are preserved (the sweep only consumes adjacent spaces, never newlines), and obvious words containing filler-like substrings ("umbrella", "umpire", etc.) are left intact because the sweep is anchored on word boundaries. When the user dictates again right after a previous dictation, Jot inserts a separating space ahead of the new text so consecutive dictations don't run together into one unbroken sentence. A deeper, AI-based cleanup that runs a saved prompt on every dictation is available as an opt-in — see Automatic Cleanup with AI; the "Transcribe Audio with Jot" Shortcuts action exposes the same pass as a per-run "Clean Up Transcript" flag.

### 7.1a Punctuation & Capitalization Restoration (English)

After the filler sweep and the number pass, English dictations are re-punctuated by a small
on-device model (punct_cap_seg, ~57 MB, downloaded automatically over Wi-Fi in the background
the first time the app runs — never bundled, never on cellular, and the app works normally
without it). It restores sentence boundaries, commas, question marks, capitalization of sentence
starts and proper nouns, and ALL-CAPS acronyms.

Why replace the recognizer's own punctuation rather than add to it: on 420 real dictations with
the words held identical and only the punctuation swapped, three independent blind judges
preferred this model over Parakeet's own punctuation 31–16 (pooled 101 vs 44). It notably
recovers acronyms the recognizer flattens — JWT, JSON, OKTA — and capitalizes product names
Parakeet leaves lower-case (Sony, Mac, Apple, Gemini, Kafka).

The transcript is stripped of case and sentence punctuation and re-punctuated wholesale rather
than layered on top; applying it over already-punctuated text roughly triples the marks
("there??", "log. File..").

chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup
chunks.text:
It notably
recovers acronyms the recognizer flattens — JWT, JSON, OKTA — and capitalizes product names
Parakeet leaves lower-case (Sony, Mac, Apple, Gemini, Kafka).

The transcript is stripped of case and sentence punctuation and re-punctuated wholesale rather
than layered on top; applying it over already-punctuated text roughly triples the marks
("there??", "log. File.."). Contractions and digit-internal separators are preserved through the
strip, so "I'm" stays "I'm" and "5,000" stays "5,000" — the model has no apostrophe label and
could never re-create the first, and would re-punctuate the second as prose.

This applies to English on both engines — a dictation routed through Apple's recognizer is
re-punctuated the same way as a Parakeet one (the strip-first design means Apple's own
punctuation is replaced, never doubled).

English only for now, and that is an evidence gate rather than a technical one. A
47-language build of the same model exists at nearly the same size and covers most of Jot's
Parakeet-routed languages; it is not enabled because the evaluation behind this feature was
English-only. The CJK rows are additionally out of scope for this particular model — its labels
are . , ? rather than 。 、, and per-character casing is meaningless for those scripts.
The live preview is also deliberately excluded: it re-runs while the user is still speaking, and
re-punctuating each tick would make sentence boundaries jump around as later words arrive.

chunks.title: AI Rewrite Engine
chunks.text: AI Rewrite Engine. AI Rewrite runs on Apple Intelligence — the same models behind the iPhone's own Writing Tools. It is Jot's only rewrite engine: every Rewrite control — the note's sparkle (§7.4), the edit bar's AI button (§3.7), the keyboard's recents-row button (§5.2) and the keyboard's Rewrite tile (§7.15) — runs one of the user's prompts itself; none of them hands the user off to the system Writing Tools menu, which iOS still offers on any selected text (§3.3). There is nothing to download and nothing to manage: the user's saved prompts (§7.7) run on the on-device model, and on iOS 27 a transcript too long for that model is sent to Apple's Private Cloud Compute instead (§7.9). A rewrite either way returns only the rewritten body — never a preamble or explanation, and never an *answer*: the dictated words are treated purely as text to transform, so a dictated question ("do you understand what I'm asking?") comes back as a cleaner question, not a reply to it. The engine needs Apple Intelligence turned on (Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri) on a supported iPhone; when it is off, the Rewrite control still shows and routes the user to the AI settings screen, which explains what to turn on (§7.10, §12.3). The former downloadable 2.5 GB rewrite model is gone; any leftover weights from an earlier version are removed automatically on first launch to give the disk back.

chunks.title: Rewrite Trigger from Detail View
chunks.text: Rewrite Trigger from Detail View. From the Transcript Detail view, the accent sparkle-circle Rewrite control in the action bar (an icon-only button, no text label) opens the Prompt Picker so the user can select which rewrite style to apply to the current transcript.

chunks.title: Prompt Picker
chunks.text: Prompt Picker. A bottom sheet lists all saved rewrite prompts, each with an icon, a name, and a short description. A subline below the prompt list header shows the word count of the source transcript being rewritten and the engine (e.g. "42 words · using Apple Intelligence"). The list contains the four built-in default prompts (Cleanup, AI prompt, Action Items, Email) plus any prompts the user has created in Settings → AI. Selecting a prompt applies it to the current transcript. Below the list, a plain centered "+ New prompt" text link opens the New Prompt sheet. A footer note clarifies that rewriting replaces the previous rewrite while leaving the original transcript untouched. See Voice Prompt for the picker's second row, which lets the user *speak* the rewrite instruction instead of picking a saved one. The picker also offers a Translate row — an on-device translate sheet that is *not* a rewrite (it does not save to the transcript).

chunks.title: Saved Prompt Management
chunks.text: Saved Prompt Management. In Settings → AI, users can view their full list of saved rewrite prompts. The screen leads with an italic serif "AI" title and a small "EXPERIMENTAL" chip to set expectations about feature maturity. Prompts can be reordered by dragging, deleted by swiping, and edited by tapping. Each prompt row shows an icon, the prompt name, and — for the four built-in defaults (Cleanup, AI prompt, Action Items, Email) — a mini before→after sample that previews what the prompt does to a representative transcript. Swiping to delete shows an alert with the prompt's name as the title (e.g. "Delete "My Prompt"?") and the message "This can't be undone." — with a destructive "Delete" button and a "Cancel" button — before the prompt is removed. A "+ New prompt" button at the bottom opens a dedicated New Prompt sheet (see 7.12). Inside the prompt editor for an existing prompt, the system prompt fills the editor as the hero element and a slim "Try this prompt" footer pill at the bottom expands upward into a result panel when tapped — showing the BEFORE transcript, an arrow with run timing, the AFTER rewrite, and Copy + Run again buttons; an "Expand" link opens a full-screen text editor for the instruction. The footer pill defaults to the user's most recent recording, and tapping the recording-name sublabel (marked with a small up/down chevron) opens a recording picker listing recent recordings with a coral checkmark on the currently selected one — picking a different recording updates the BEFORE block and what Run rewrites. A spoken instruction from the Prompt Picker's Voice Prompt row never appears in this list — it applies once and is discarded.

chunks.title: Engine Status
chunks.text: Engine Status. Within Settings → AI, a single compact engine strip shows "Apple Intelligence" with a coloured-dot readiness line: "Ready · on your iPhone" when the on-device model is available, "Ready · uses Private Cloud Compute" when only Apple's cloud model can serve (iOS 27), or the one-line reason it can't run — Apple Intelligence turned off, an unsupported iPhone, or the system still setting up — with a Settings shortcut that opens iOS Settings so the user can turn it on. There is no download, progress, reload, retry or delete: Jot owns no model.

chunks.title: Private Cloud Compute Fallback
chunks.text: Private Cloud Compute Fallback. On iOS 27, a rewrite that would not fit the on-device model's context — a long recording — is sent to Apple's Private Cloud Compute instead of failing, with the same prompt and the same output contract. Jot budgets the transcript against the on-device model before starting, so the long ones go straight to the cloud model rather than failing first. Private Cloud Compute is Apple's server-side Apple Intelligence: requests are end-to-end encrypted, never stored, and not readable by Apple or by Jot, and Apple publishes the software for independent verification (§13.1). It needs a network connection and is subject to Apple's per-account daily allowance (§14.6); the AI settings footer states when a rewrite may use it. Below iOS 27 a transcript too long for the on-device model simply reports a rewrite error (§12.4). Apple grants Private Cloud Compute to an app by request; until Jot's access is granted the cloud route is not used at all, and a too-long transcript reports that same rewrite error on iOS 27 too (§14.6).

chunks.title: Setup Routing from Rewrite
chunks.text:
Setup Routing from Rewrite. When the user taps the Rewrite action in the Transcript Detail view and either Apple Intelligence is unavailable or there are no saved prompts yet, the tap routes to the AI settings screen as a sheet — the engine strip explains what to turn on (§7.8) and the prompt list can be seeded — without losing the user's place in the transcript. Settings is the only setup destination, so the user sees the same screen whether they arrived from the action bar or the AI row in Settings. The prompt list comes pre-populated with four default prompts the first time the user opens Settings → AI, in order: Cleanup (rewrite a dictation for clarity — connect related ideas so they flow logically, cut repeated points while keeping every distinct idea the speaker mentioned, and fix obvious dictation errors), AI prompt (convert a rambling dictation into a clean, well-structured prompt the speaker can paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or any other LLM — output is organized into Context / Task / Requirements / Output sections, preserving every concrete detail while cutting filler), Action Items (extract tasks from a dictation, list each as a one-line task with the responsible person if mentioned, and include any deadlines), and Email (convert a dictation into a business email with a Bottom-Line-Up-Front opening and a one-line subject line). These defaults are seeded only when the list is completely empty: if the user deletes some prompts but keeps at least one, the deleted defaults do not return; if the user deletes all prompts, the defaults reappear the next time they open Settings → AI (because the empty-list guard triggers again). The Transcript Detail view does not add default prompts on its own — it only routes to Settings.

Rewrites that start without a picker: the keyboard's recents-row Rewrite button opens the note and runs the Cleanup prompt straight away (a note that already has a rewrite simply opens on its Rewrite tab).

chunks.title: Setup Routing from Rewrite
chunks.text:
These defaults are seeded only when the list is completely empty: if the user deletes some prompts but keeps at least one, the deleted defaults do not return; if the user deletes all prompts, the defaults reappear the next time they open Settings → AI (because the empty-list guard triggers again). The Transcript Detail view does not add default prompts on its own — it only routes to Settings.

Rewrites that start without a picker: the keyboard's recents-row Rewrite button opens the note and runs the Cleanup prompt straight away (a note that already has a rewrite simply opens on its Rewrite tab). (The edit bar's AI button is not one of these: it opens the same prompt picker as the sparkle and rewrites the draft in place with whichever prompt is chosen.) The recents-row button follows the same rule as the sparkle: with Apple Intelligence off they route to the AI settings sheet instead (§12.3). Jot no longer has a "Writing Tools" engine, a read-only selection mode or a guide that pointed users at the system menu — iOS's Writing Tools remain available on any selected text (§3.3), but nothing in Jot depends on them.

chunks.title: New Prompt Sheet
chunks.text: New Prompt Sheet. Creating a new rewrite prompt opens a dedicated sheet, distinct from the editor used for existing prompts (7.7). The sheet shows a name field, a selectable icon picker (8 colored tiles — the selected tile is enlarged with a white-then-color ring), a mono system-prompt editor with a helpful placeholder ("Describe how Jot should transform the selected text. Tip: be specific about voice, length, and what to preserve. Test on a recording before saving."), and a "Start from a template" footer offering four one-tap starters: "Translate to…", "Make it shorter", "More formal", and "Action items". Tapping a template chip fills the editor with a canned starter prompt and switches the icon to match. The Save button is disabled until both the name and the system prompt have content. Saved prompts land at the bottom of the prompt list and persist via the same store used by everything else in §7.7.

chunks.title: Voice Prompt
chunks.text: Voice Prompt. The second row of the Prompt Picker — "Voice prompt · Say what to change." (mic icon) — lets the user dictate a one-off rewrite instruction instead of picking a saved prompt. Tapping the row immediately starts recording and the sheet switches to a minimal capture view: a pulsing "Listening…" line, the words appearing live as they're spoken, a prominent Stop button, and an X to cancel. The user says what they want changed ("make this shorter and turn it into an email to Sam") and taps Stop; the dictated instruction then drives the same rewrite that a saved prompt would, and the result lands on the Rewrite tab as usual. Cancel (or dismissing the sheet mid-recording) stops the mic and drops the audio without rewriting; if nothing intelligible was captured, the picker returns with a "Didn't catch that — try again." note. The spoken instruction is used once and is not saved — it does not appear in Saved Prompt Management, and no transcript of it is added to Home & Library. The row is disabled while another recording is in progress; a Warm Hold idle mic does not count as in-progress, and the capture honours Warm Hold on stop like every other recording surface.

chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup with AI
chunks.text: Automatic Cleanup with AI. An opt-in — the AI cleanup card in Settings → AI (a sparkles tile in the same glass card and row style as the rest of Settings) with a "Clean up every dictation" toggle, off by default, or the Cleanup tile in the keyboard's actions pane, which flips the same setting without opening the app — runs one of the user's saved prompts on every fresh dictation right after transcription, so what comes out is already polished. A Prompt row picks which saved prompt runs (any prompt from §7.7; the built-in Cleanup prompt by default, and edits to that prompt apply to future dictations). A second toggle, "Paste the cleaned-up text" (on by default), decides what the keyboard pastes: on, the keyboard's strip and Jot down button and the in-app recording surface say "Cleaning up" for a few seconds (§5.5, §2.5) and the cleaned text is pasted — the wait is capped at about twenty seconds, after which the raw words paste and the cleanup finishes in the background instead; off, the raw transcript pastes immediately, the note's row shows a small "Cleaning up" spinner (§1.2), and the cleaned version fades into the note's Rewrite tab a few seconds later. Either way the note's attribution line then reads "Cleaned up automatically with “Cleanup”" (or whichever prompt ran). Cleanup only ever rephrases: a dictated question or request stays a question or request and is never answered (§7.2). Either way the raw words stay on the Original tab and the cleaned text is the note's rewrite, exactly as a manual rewrite would leave it. The cleanup runs on Apple Intelligence — on the iPhone, with the Private Cloud Compute fallback for a dictation too long for the on-device model on iOS 27 — and needs Apple Intelligence on (the card dims and its first row says "Needs Apple Intelligence — turn it on above" until it is); if it is unavailable or fails, the raw transcript is pasted and saved as usual, never lost, and the keyboard's status row says "Cleanup didn't run — pasted as spoken".

chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup with AI
chunks.text: The cleanup runs on Apple Intelligence — on the iPhone, with the Private Cloud Compute fallback for a dictation too long for the on-device model on iOS 27 — and needs Apple Intelligence on (the card dims and its first row says "Needs Apple Intelligence — turn it on above" until it is); if it is unavailable or fails, the raw transcript is pasted and saved as usual, never lost, and the keyboard's status row says "Cleanup didn't run — pasted as spoken". One failure is handled differently: after a burst of dictations from the keyboard, the iPhone can limit AI work for an app that is in the background, and the cleanup would fail every time until that limit lifts. Instead of failing, the words paste as spoken right away, the status row says "Pasted as spoken — cleanup will finish when you open Jot", and the cleanup runs the next time Jot is opened — the note's row shows "Cleaning up" while it does (§1.2) and the cleaned text then lands in the Rewrite tab with the usual attribution. Nothing waits or retries in the background; a cleanup that is neither finished nor deferred stays a plain paste. Every failed or deferred cleanup is listed with its reason in Diagnostics (§6.5, §12.3). It applies to dictations from the keyboard, the in-app Dictate button, the Action Button and the Apple Watch, to audio shared via Send to Jot, and (as the per-run flag) to the Shortcuts file action. It does not run on a dictation stopped inside one of Jot's own fields (nothing is saved there), and a chained follow-up command already cleans as part of applying the command, so it is not cleaned twice.

chunks.title: Rewrite the Selection from the Keyboard
chunks.text: Rewrite the Selection from the Keyboard. Select text in any app's field, open the keyboard's actions pane and tap Rewrite: the pane closes, the status banner shows "Rewriting…", and a few seconds later the selection is replaced in place by the rewritten text — no trip to Jot, no menus. It runs the same prompt as Automatic Cleanup with AI (the chosen saved prompt, else the built-in Cleanup) on Apple's on-device model, so nothing leaves the iPhone; the banner then reads "Rewritten — Undo brings back your words", and the pane's Undo restores the original selection exactly. If the selection changes or the field loses focus while the model is working, nothing is written ("Selection changed — rewrite not applied"); if the model takes longer than about twenty seconds or fails, the selection is left untouched and the banner says why. Needs Apple Intelligence on (§7.2); without it the tile is washed and a tap says "Turn on Apple Intelligence in Settings to rewrite here". Without Full Access the keyboard can't read the saved prompts, so the built-in Cleanup prompt runs.

chunks.title: Translate the Selection from the Keyboard
chunks.text: Translate the Selection from the Keyboard. Select text in any app's field, open the keyboard's actions pane and tap Translate: a "Translate to" row of language chips appears — the same languages as the app's Translate sheet, with the selection's own (detected) language left out and the last language used first. Tapping a chip closes the pane, the status banner shows "Translating to Spanish…", and the selection is replaced in place by the translation ("Translated to Spanish — Undo brings back your words"); the pane's Undo restores the original exactly. Translation runs entirely on the iPhone with the system's built-in translation, so nothing leaves the device (§13.1) — which also means a language pack has to be on the phone: languages already downloaded show as bright chips, the rest are dimmed with a download glyph, and tapping one explains that translating a note to that language once in Jot (§3.9) downloads it (the keyboard can't show the system's download prompt). If the selection changes while translating, nothing is written; if it takes longer than about twenty seconds or fails, the selection is left untouched and the banner says why.

chunks.title: Custom Term List
chunks.text:
Custom Term List. Users can maintain a list of domain-specific words, names, or technical terms that Jot should recognize correctly during transcription. The list is managed from Settings → Vocabulary. Each term can have editable "sounds like" forms — misheard spellings that Jot corrects toward it — learned through Find & Replace, correction prompts. Vocabulary biasing applies on either dictation engine — Apple's or Jot's own — for every language except Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese. Vocabulary is no longer offered as an onboarding step — it lives only in Settings.

### 8.1a Learn from Corrections
Correct a wrong word once, any way, and the next dictation writes it. Every way of fixing a word counts as the same correction — "when I say *cloud*, write *Claude*": editing the transcript's Original text and tapping Save (Jot compares what was on screen with what was saved and learns the short word swaps, like "cloud" → "Claude"; edits on the Rewrite tab teach nothing, because the AI wrote that text), selecting a word and choosing Add to Vocabulary (in a transcript or from the keyboard's "…" menu), picking the term in the transcript's review list, answering a keyboard review card, accepting Find & Replace's add-to-vocabulary offer, or typing a sounds-like in Settings. Each correction is saved once, visibly: the term goes in the list (if it isn't there already) and the misheard form becomes one of its "sounds like" chips in Settings → Vocabulary. Deleting that chip undoes it; the review list's Undo reverses exactly what one correction added. Jot only learns from edits that look like a misheard name or term — a one-to-three-word swap for a one-to-four-word replacement that sounds alike; rewording ("tomorrow" → "on Monday"), grammar swaps between everyday words ("their" → "there"), and number or punctuation edits teach nothing, and a case-only fix ("claude" → "Claude") just corrects the term's spelling.

chunks.title: Custom Term List
chunks.text: Jot only learns from edits that look like a misheard name or term — a one-to-three-word swap for a one-to-four-word replacement that sounds alike; rewording ("tomorrow" → "on Monday"), grammar swaps between everyday words ("their" → "there"), and number or punctuation edits teach nothing, and a case-only fix ("claude" → "Claude") just corrects the term's spelling. Changing a term back to what Jot originally heard (or choosing keep original) pauses that pair: Jot stops proposing it, the sounds-like stays listed. There are no hidden replace rules and no "always replace" — a word only changes when what was said supports it; learning never makes Jot swap words blindly. Edit learning runs for languages with an everyday-word list (English and the major European languages).

chunks.title: Vocabulary Empty State
chunks.text: Vocabulary Empty State. When no terms have been added, the vocabulary screen shows a dedicated empty state inviting the user to add their first term.

chunks.title: Term Addition
chunks.text:
Term Addition. There are two paths for adding a term:

Primary — floating "Add term" button. A floating action button is always visible at the bottom of the Vocabulary screen (hovering above the list). Tapping it opens a dedicated modal sheet titled "New term" — a half-height sheet with a form for entering the new term text.

Secondary — inline "Add Term" row. An "Add Term" row is also present at the bottom of the terms list (visible both in normal and Edit mode). Tapping it inserts a blank term inline and focuses the text field immediately, without opening a sheet.

Terms added via either path are applied to subsequent transcriptions only when the Vocabulary Boost toggle is on. The vocabulary boost model is not part of the app download — enabling vocabulary fetches it once, on demand — but terms start working immediately either way, because Jot also matches them against the finished transcript without needing any model (§8.9). Anyone who had vocabulary working before updating keeps it working with no re-download.

chunks.title: Term Editing and Ordering
chunks.text: Term Editing and Ordering. Within the Vocabulary settings screen, terms can be reordered by dragging, deleted by swiping, and the list can be switched into an edit mode for bulk management. Each existing term row is always an inline text field — there is no separate edit-mode-only state or tap-to-reveal gesture. Tapping the term places the cursor and lets the user edit it immediately. Learned sounds-like forms — every correction the user has made, wherever they made it — appear beneath the term as removable chips with an "add a misheard form…" field beside them; removing a chip undoes that correction, and deleting or renaming a term takes its sounds-likes with it — the row is shown for every term, whether or not it has any yet, so the list always looks like the editable thing it is. Teach it by voice offers an optional guided way to discover those forms from Jot's actual recognition mistakes; it appears only when vocabulary is switched on and the current dictation language uses it.

chunks.title: Term Quality Warnings
chunks.text: Term Quality Warnings. As a term is typed, a short orange line under it explains a problem: "Too short" for two characters or fewer (such terms are skipped), or — using the everyday-word list of the current dictation language — that the term's first word is an everyday word (or, in English, that it opens with one, like "And…" in "Andalamma"), so Jot may mix it up with ordinary speech. The same rule is used by Jot for Mac and Windows.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Boost Toggle
chunks.text: Vocabulary Boost Toggle. A master toggle in the Vocabulary settings screen enables or disables vocabulary boosting entirely, letting users compare transcription with and without their term list without deleting the list itself. While the toggle is off, the keyboard may show a one-time Vocabulary setup nudge inviting the user to turn it on — the nudge routes here; nothing is ever enabled automatically.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Model Status
chunks.text: Vocabulary Model Status. The vocabulary boost is powered by a small additional on-device model (~99 MB) that improves recognition of the user's saved terms *while it listens*. It is not part of the app download: enabling vocabulary fetches it once, with a progress row, and the listening-time boost starts as soon as it lands. Until then the terms are still corrected in the finished transcript (§8.9) rather than doing nothing, and the Vocabulary settings screen says honestly which of the two is running — the rest of Jot keeps working meanwhile. Anyone who already had vocabulary working before updating keeps it working with no re-download.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Correction Prompts in the Keyboard
chunks.text: Vocabulary Correction Prompts in the Keyboard. After a dictation, when Jot has a candidate correction tied to the user's custom vocabulary — a spot where it suspects a heard word should have been one of the user's saved terms — the Jot Keyboard holds the paste and shows a small review card before inserting (up to three, one question at a time), so the user picks the right word *before* it lands in the field. The keyboard only prompts about corrections it actually made, or a mapping it's already learning — guesses it judged an unlikely match for what was said are never turned into a keyboard prompt (they still appear in the transcript for review, so nothing is lost). This keeps the prompts from nagging about words that don't sound like the heard term. Each card offers the heard word or the saved term — and, when the user's list has a longer term that also fits (they saved both "Claude" and "Claude Code" and said the longer one), a third choice for it, so the right word is one tap away even when two saved terms compete for the same phrase. A Stop asking option and a short countdown ring round out the card; if the user doesn't answer, Jot inserts its best guess and moves on — and if they don't engage the first card at all, it inserts right away rather than make them wait. Whatever the user picks is what gets pasted. While cards are up the text is still waiting to land, so the Jot down button is unavailable until they're answered — starting a second dictation over a paste that hasn't happened yet would lose the first one. Leaving the keyboard mid-question and coming back picks up on the same card, with earlier answers kept. Jot also learns from the answers: once the user has kept the original word a couple of times for a given suggestion, the keyboard stops asking about it (it still appears in the transcript for review in the app, so nothing is lost), and Stop asking silences one immediately.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Correction Prompts in the Keyboard
chunks.text: Leaving the keyboard mid-question and coming back picks up on the same card, with earlier answers kept. Jot also learns from the answers: once the user has kept the original word a couple of times for a given suggestion, the keyboard stops asking about it (it still appears in the transcript for review in the app, so nothing is lost), and Stop asking silences one immediately. Two special cases: when the recognizer split one word into several ("Sriram" heard as "sri ram"), Jot offers a one-time teaching card after the paste (never delaying it) — confirming writes the misheard form as a sounds-like so future dictations get it right. Every answer is a correction: picking the term saves the heard form as a visible sounds-like on it, keeping the original (or Stop asking) pauses that pair, and a card left to time out teaches nothing. Nothing is ever applied automatically because of past answers — there is no "always replace". These prompts and the confirmations the user gives are private and stay on the device — nothing about them leaves the iPhone. The corrections feed the user's vocabulary and are independent of the Vocabulary Boost toggle's on/off state for biasing. The same heard→term learning is also fed when the user fixes a repeatedly-misheard word with Find & Replace and accepts its add-to-vocabulary offer.

chunks.title: Vocabulary Without the Download
chunks.text: Vocabulary Without the Download. Jot corrects the user's saved terms in two ways, and the second needs nothing extra. The first listens to the audio and needs the vocabulary boost model; the second reads the finished transcript and matches it against the term list directly, so it works with no download, no wait, and in far more languages. Both run on every dictation and are weighed together: a close spelling match claims its words first, and a listening match is placed on the exact word Jot wrote at the moment it was heard (never guessed from its position in the recording). Every correction then passes the same safety checks. In practice this means saved terms start being corrected the moment they are added, and keep being corrected in languages the listening boost was never trained for. It is deliberately cautious: it will not rewrite an everyday word, a possessive ("Mariana's"), or a correctly-spelled word that merely resembles a saved term, and it is switched off entirely for languages where Jot has not measured it as safe rather than guessing. Whatever it corrects shows up in the same transcript review and keyboard prompts as everything else, so the user always sees and can undo it, and it is governed by the same Vocabulary Boost toggle. Jot never learns to replace an everyday word: confirming a change such as "not → Jot" is not remembered as a rule, such questions are not asked, and rules like that learned by older versions are removed once. When the keyboard asks about corrections, the ones resting only on spelling come first, since they are the likeliest to be wrong.

chunks.title: Help Screen
chunks.text: Help Screen. A structured, scannable help reference accessible from the home header or from Settings → About — presented as a modal sheet from home or a navigation push from Settings. It opens on "What Jot does" (§9.7), a tap-to-expand showcase of Jot's main features, followed by a How Jot works row that pushes §9.2, a collapsible Troubleshooting section (§9.5), a Privacy row that pushes §9.4, and a Send feedback row (§9.6). This screen is the browsable form of the same product knowledge that Ask Jot answers conversationally.

chunks.title: How Jot Works
chunks.text: How Jot Works. A dedicated page (pushed from the Help screen's "How Jot works" row) walks through the basic Jot workflow — tap Dictate on the keyboard, Jot opens and starts recording, swipe back to the app, stop from the keyboard — as four numbered steps beside an animated mini-phone scene reused from the Setup Wizard (W5). An honest footnote explains the app-switch: iOS doesn't let keyboards use the mic directly, so Jot hops to the foreground to capture; if that ever changes, the hop goes away. Honors Reduce Motion (the animation freezes on its final frame).

chunks.title: AI Rewrite Guide
chunks.text: AI Rewrite Guide. The optional AI Rewrite feature is explained inline as the expandable body of the "Polish what you said" feature row on the Help screen (no longer a standalone section). It describes tapping Rewrite on any transcript in the Transcript Detail view to apply Cleanup, Translate, Action Items, Email, or a custom prompt — fully on-device. Earlier copy advertising a keyboard "wand" entry point has been removed: rewriting is triggered from the transcript, not the keyboard (see §7.3).

chunks.title: Privacy Explainer
chunks.text: Privacy Explainer. A dedicated "See for yourself" page (pushed from the Help screen's Privacy row) summarises where Jot processes the user's words — dictation on the iPhone, Ask and long rewrites in Apple's Private Cloud Compute, no accounts, no telemetry — and teaches the user to *verify* it with iOS's own App Privacy Report: a static preview lists the short set of domains Jot contacts (model downloads; Apple's Private Cloud Compute on iOS 27; the donations/feedback page) with a plain-language caption per row, plus an Open Settings button. Because iOS exposes no deep link into the App Privacy Report, a footnote gives the manual path (Privacy & Security › App Privacy Report). The one exception to "nothing leaves the device" — tapping Send Feedback — is named here; Full Access rationale stays in the Setup Wizard and Settings → Privacy. The iOS system-Settings privacy helper (§13.6a) points users to this same App Privacy Report to verify the on-device claim. See also §13.1.

chunks.title: Collapsible Troubleshooting
chunks.text: Collapsible Troubleshooting. A Troubleshooting section in Help contains collapsible Q&A entries addressing the most common issues: the keyboard didn't paste, the recording was cut off unexpectedly, the speech model didn't load, and the transcription produced wrong words. Each entry is collapsed by default to keep the screen scannable.

chunks.title: Feedback Contact
chunks.text: Feedback Contact. A Contact section at the bottom of the Help screen provides a Send feedback button that opens an in-app feedback form. The form has a text field, an "Add screenshots" button (multi-select up to 3 from the user's photo library — each thumbnail is shown below the editor with an X button to remove individually), and an "Include diagnostic logs" toggle (default off; when on, attaches a recent slice of anonymous app events — recording start/stop, paste outcomes, memory warnings — to help track down bugs; an explicit caption reassures that no personal info or transcripts are included). A counter shows the combined screenshot size and current selection count so the user can see what they're about to upload. The app version and platform are attached automatically. The user stays inside Jot — no Mail handoff. After a successful send the form auto-clears (text, screenshots, and the logs toggle all reset) and a green-check "Sent. Thank you." confirmation appears in place for fifteen seconds before fading on its own — so the user can immediately type another piece of feedback without needing to dismiss anything, and a stale confirmation never lingers. The Send button is disabled while a submission is in flight so repeated taps can't fire duplicate uploads. On rate-limit or server errors the message is shown inline so the user can try again. The same form is reachable from Settings → About → Send feedback (see §6.5 About).

chunks.title: What Jot Does
chunks.text: What Jot Does. The first section of the Help screen — a card of four tap-to-expand feature rows, each framed as a user situation with a short body revealed on tap. Speak instead of typing, in any app (switch to the Jot keyboard, tap Jot down, talk; the words land in the focused field). Keep going when life interrupts describes the warm-hold microphone staying ready across app switches and incoming calls, with continuous saves so partial dictations survive. Polish what you said into what you meant describes tapping Rewrite on any transcript to apply Cleanup, Translate, Action Items, Email, or a custom prompt. Find your ideas by asking Jot describes Ask Jot — asking in plain words and getting an answer drawn from your own notes. A hint line invites the user to tap a feature to read how it works.

chunks.title: Shortcuts: Transcribe Audio with Jot
chunks.text: Shortcuts: Transcribe Audio with Jot. Jot exposes a Shortcuts action — "Transcribe Audio with Jot" — that accepts an audio file as input and returns a transcript string as output. The action runs in the background without opening the app, appends the result to the transcript history, and returns the raw transcript by default. Unlike the recording screen and keyboard, this surface does NOT run the Automatic Cleanup pass — cleanup on the Shortcuts file action is gated solely on the per-run "Clean Up Transcript" toggle described next. An optional "Clean Up Transcript" toggle applies a separate cleanup pass (Apple Intelligence based, distinct from the bundled cleanup model used elsewhere) to the output; if that pass is unavailable or fails, the shortcut silently falls back to returning the raw transcript (no error is surfaced to the Shortcuts automation). This action is chainable with other Shortcuts steps — for example, after the system "Record Audio" action — making it useful for batch workflows or automation pipelines.

chunks.title: Action Button Shortcut
chunks.text: Action Button Shortcut. Jot exposes a "Jot down a note" action (Action Button label: "Jot down") in Apple's Shortcuts app that can be assigned to the iPhone's Action Button (or invoked from any Shortcuts automation). When triggered, it briefly brings Jot to the foreground to start recording — iOS does not allow a background process to start microphone capture — then a second press stops recording, transcribes, and copies the result to the clipboard. The action is discoverable in the Action Button settings under the Shortcuts category.

chunks.title: Deep Link Routing
chunks.text: Deep Link Routing. Jot supports deep links that open the app directly into a new recording session or bring the app to the foreground aimed at the transcript library. These links can be triggered from other apps, web pages, or Shortcuts. The library deep link does not force a navigation reset — if a sheet or other navigation is already open when the link fires, the user will not automatically land on the library view.

chunks.title: Shortcuts: Save a Note
chunks.text: Shortcuts: Save a Note. Jot exposes a "Save a Note" Shortcuts action that takes a piece of text and saves it straight into the transcript library — no recording involved. It runs headless (without opening the app) and is chainable, so any Shortcut step that produces text — a dictation in another app, a clipboard value, an earlier action's output — can drop a note into Jot. Fully on-device.

chunks.title: Shortcuts: Ask Your Notes
chunks.text: Shortcuts: Ask Your Notes. Jot exposes an "Ask Your Notes" Shortcuts action that takes a spoken or typed question and returns a short answer drawn from the user's own transcripts — the same Ask Jot engine, reachable from the Shortcuts app without opening Jot. The action runs headless and returns its answer as plain spoken-style prose with no citation chips (there is nowhere to render them on that surface). Useful for a quick hands-free "what did I say about…?" — see §14.8.

chunks.title: Share Sheet: Send to Jot
chunks.text: Share Sheet: Send to Jot. Jot is a native destination in iOS's Share Sheet for audio files — no Shortcut needed. From any app that has an audio file (Files, Voice Memos, Mail attachments, and similar), tapping Share and choosing Jot queues the file and shows a brief "Saved to Jot" confirmation without opening the app. The next time Jot is opened normally, it transcribes every queued file in the background and adds each one to the transcript library — no manual step needed to complete the import. If a shared file has more than one voice (for example a call recording), Jot also splits it into speaker turns automatically as part of this import, so a multi-voice clip arrives already carrying its Speakers tab; this never blocks or delays the import, and a single-voice file is unaffected. Jot only appears in the share sheet for audio; sharing anything else (photos, links, documents) does not offer Jot as a target. Fully on-device, like every other transcription surface. When Automatic Cleanup with AI is on, a shared recording's transcript is cleaned the same way a dictation is.

chunks.title: Recording Start Haptic
chunks.text: Recording Start Haptic. A haptic pulse fires when a recording session begins, providing tactile confirmation that the microphone is active — useful when the phone is not in view.

chunks.title: Recording Stop Haptic
chunks.text: Recording Stop Haptic. A distinct haptic fires when the user taps the stop button, confirming the recording has ended.

chunks.title: Cancel Haptic
chunks.text: Cancel Haptic. Cancelling a recording mid-session produces its own haptic, differentiating the "nothing saved" outcome from the "saved successfully" stop.

chunks.title: Success Haptic
chunks.text: Success Haptic. A success haptic fires after transcription completes and the result is saved, marking the moment the transcript becomes available in the library.

chunks.title: Keyboard Input-Click and Haptic Feedback
chunks.text: Keyboard Input-Click and Haptic Feedback. Taps on the Jot keyboard produce audio and haptic feedback that matches the feel of the native iOS keyboard. The keyboard is recording-controls-only — there are no letter, number, punctuation, or space keys; the single typing key is the adaptive Enter key (whose label mirrors the system return key by context — see §5.1). Pressing Enter plays the standard iOS keyboard click sound paired with a light tap; the recording controls (Pause, Cancel) and the Actions button play a system-style click paired with a selection-style haptic. Stop is the one exception — it plays a medium impact haptic only, with no audio click. Requires Full Access; without it both audio and haptics are silently suppressed.

chunks.title: Microphone Permission Denied
chunks.text: Microphone Permission Denied. If microphone access is denied, the Setup Wizard surfaces a deep-link to iOS Settings. In the main app, denied permission surfaces an alert dialog with a single OK button that dismisses the alert; there is no Settings deep link from this alert, so the user must navigate to iOS Settings manually to grant microphone access. In the keyboard, errors including permission issues surface via the status banner.

chunks.title: Model Download Failure
chunks.text: Model Download Failure. For English, dictation defaults to Apple's on-device engine, which needs no download, so the default English path can't hit this. Two downloads can: choosing a European language fetches the separate multilingual model (§6.1), and switching to Jot's own more-accurate English engine (§6.1) fetches that engine if it isn't already present. Either way a failed or interrupted download surfaces in place with a "Download failed" message and a retry button. (AI Rewrite and Ask need no download — see §12.3 for what happens when Apple Intelligence isn't available.)

chunks.title: Apple Intelligence Unavailable
chunks.text: Apple Intelligence Unavailable. AI Rewrite and Ask run on Apple Intelligence, so the failure mode is not a download but the system being off or unsupported. In the Transcript Detail view, tapping Rewrite while Apple Intelligence is off routes the user to the AI settings sheet, whose engine strip states the reason and offers a Settings shortcut — see §7.10; the edit bar's AI button and a rewrite started from the keyboard's recents row follow the same rule, and the keyboard's own Rewrite and Cleanup tiles explain it in the status banner instead. Ask never shows its entry point in that state (§14.6); if Apple Intelligence is turned off or the daily Private Cloud Compute allowance runs out while the sheet is open, Ask explains it in place with an Open Settings / See options button. An error card appears only after a rewrite attempt actually fails (see §12.4). A separate, temporary limit applies to automatic cleanup after a burst of keyboard dictations, when the iPhone throttles AI work for an app in the background: that is not a failure the user has to act on — the words paste as spoken and the cleanup completes the next time Jot is opened. Failed and deferred cleanups, with their reasons, are listed in Diagnostics (§6.5).

chunks.title: Rewrite Error
chunks.text: Rewrite Error. If a rewrite fails mid-generation (a model error, a refused request, or — on iOS 27, when the transcript went to Private Cloud Compute — a network problem), the Transcript Detail view shows an error card the user can dismiss. If the user cancels the in-progress rewrite, the view returns silently to idle — no error card is shown for user-initiated cancellation. The original transcript is never modified by a failed or cancelled rewrite.

chunks.title: Keyboard Status Banner
chunks.text: Keyboard Status Banner. Transient errors inside the Jot Keyboard — such as a transcription failure or a missing model — are communicated via an overlay banner that appears without requiring the user to leave the host app. Non-rewriting banners auto-clear approximately 2.5 seconds after they render; the "Rewriting…" banner persists until the rewriting state changes.

chunks.title: Where Your Words Are Processed
chunks.text: Where Your Words Are Processed. Speech recognition and transcription run entirely on the iPhone: no audio ever leaves the device. Text features use Apple Intelligence. AI Rewrite runs on the on-device model; on iOS 27 a transcript too long for it is sent to Apple's Private Cloud Compute (§7.9). Ask Jot always uses Private Cloud Compute (iOS 27): the question, the notes Ask reads to answer it, and the answer travel to Apple's servers. Private Cloud Compute is Apple's privacy-preserving cloud for Apple Intelligence — requests are end-to-end encrypted, processed on Apple silicon servers that keep no data after the response, are not accessible to Apple or to Jot, and run software Apple publishes for independent security researchers to verify. Jot itself runs no servers and receives nothing. This is surfaced in Settings → Privacy, the AI settings footer, and the Help screen.

chunks.title: Warm Hold
chunks.text:
Warm Hold. When enabled (opt-in during wizard step W7 or via Settings → Privacy), Jot keeps the audio session active after a recording ends to reduce latency at the start of the next dictation. The duration is configurable in Settings → Privacy: it defaults to 2 minutes, offers 60s, 2 min, 3 min, 5 min, and 30 min choices, and can be set up to a maximum of 30 min. The toggle is clearly labeled and off by default. During the warm-hold window the iOS orange microphone indicator remains visible and the audio session stays active; no audio is captured or retained. The same held-but-not-capturing behavior backs Pause / Resume mid-dictation (the orange indicator stays on while paused, but paused audio is dropped, never captured or stored). Stopping a Voice Prompt capture honours Warm Hold like every other recording surface.

Yielding the mic to other apps. Warm Hold never blocks anything else from using the microphone. If another app needs audio during the warm window — you take a call, join a Teams/Zoom/FaceTime meeting, play a video, or start a Voice Memo — Jot immediately steps aside and hands the microphone over, so the other app works normally. Jot silently reclaims the warm session the next time you dictate, with nothing required from the user. (Earlier builds could hold the session in a state that prevented other apps from playing or recording audio during the warm window; Jot now always relinquishes on demand and re-acquires on the next dictation.)

UI-path difference during Warm Hold: when the user taps Dictate in the keyboard while a warm-hold session is still active, the keyboard recognizes the active window and recording starts immediately — Jot is not brought to the foreground. The user stays in the host app for the full dictation; only the keyboard's streaming strip (§5.3) animates to show live progress. When the recording finishes and transcription completes, the text is auto-pasted as normal.

chunks.title: Full Access Disclosure
chunks.text: Full Access Disclosure. The Setup Wizard explains why Full Access is required for the keyboard: it allows the keyboard to access the transcript result produced by the main app in order to paste it into the host app. The Help screen does not explain the Full Access rationale — it mentions Full Access only in a troubleshooting entry directing users to enable it when paste does not work. The Settings → Privacy section includes a tappable Full Access row that opens iOS Settings to Jot's app-settings page (with a subline that gives the navigation breadcrumb to Allow Full Access); no status chip is shown because iOS does not expose Full Access state to the main app. After setup, if the user is using the keyboard and Full Access has not been granted, the keyboard surfaces a locked-state "Enable Full Access" pill that opens iOS Settings to the same page. The reason this opens the app-settings page rather than the keyboard panel directly: Apple's QA1924 prefs: URL would land closer to the toggle, but on iOS 26 it returns success: true from extensionContext.open while doing nothing — so we use the documented public URL that reliably opens. The iOS system Settings page for Jot also carries a "Don't see 'Keyboards' settings?" helper and a privacy explainer (see §13.6a).

chunks.title: Transcript Storage
chunks.text:
Transcript Storage. Transcripts are stored locally on the device. Users can delete individual transcripts via the swipe or context menu on the home screen or via the Delete action in the Transcript Detail view. There is no active cross-device iCloud sync — each device's library is independent. For manual backup and restore independent of iCloud, see §6.8 Your Data (Export & Import).

iCloud Device Backup behavior. When the user has iCloud Backup enabled in iOS Settings, the following are included in their device backup automatically: transcripts (Original + Rewrite), saved AI Rewrite prompts, custom vocabulary, and app preferences. Source audio is retained on-device for up to 3 days to allow re-transcription, but it is explicitly EXCLUDED from iCloud Backup so it never bloats the backup (and it is deleted automatically once the 3-day window elapses). None of Jot's downloadable models ride the backup. English dictation uses Apple's own on-device engine (nothing of Jot's to back up); Jot's optional models — the more-accurate English engine, the multilingual model for European languages, and the vocabulary boost model — are each kept out of the backup and either carry forward from a prior install or re-download on first use after a restore, rather than bloating it (typical Jot backup size: a few MB, not GB). AI Rewrite and Ask use Apple Intelligence, so there is no rewrite model of Jot's to back up. The Settings → About card surfaces a static "Backed up with iCloud (when iCloud Backup is enabled in iOS Settings)" row so users can confirm this expectation at a glance.

On restore (full device setup from an iCloud backup → Jot reinstalled), the library returns to the state it was in at the moment the backup was taken. Restoring a single app from the App Store does NOT bring its data back — only full-device "Restore from iCloud Backup" does.

Schema changes carry explicit version migrations (see docs/schema-migrations.md), so restoring an old backup on a newer build of Jot loads cleanly via the migration plan.

chunks.title: Rewrite Edit Training Pairs
chunks.text:
Rewrite Edit Training Pairs. When the user manually edits the Rewrite tab text via Edit Transcript, Jot keeps both the model's original rewrite output AND the user's edited version on-device. The pair — what the model produced and what the user changed it to — is preserved as a future-improvement signal for Jot's rewrite prompts. The optional 👍 / 👎 rating from Rewrite Feedback is stored alongside the pair as a rating-without-correction signal. Nothing about any of this is uploaded; it stays in the same local store as the rest of the user's transcripts and is included in iCloud Device Backup like other user data. Tapping Rewrite on a transcript clears any prior user-edit AND rating (a stale correction or rating against a fresh model output would be meaningless), and discarding the rewrite clears all three together.

### 13.6a iOS Settings Helper (System Settings → Jot)
The iOS system Settings page for Jot (Settings → Jot, below the system permission toggles) carries two help blocks — the same place a user lands when hunting for the Keyboards toggle. The first, "Don't see 'Keyboards' settings?", tells the user to close and reopen Settings, or to open the Jot app and follow Settings → Privacy → Full Access (breadcrumb: General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Jot → Allow Full Access). The second, "Your privacy is protected," leads with a clean main claim — "Nothing you say is ever sent anywhere Apple or Jot can read it." — and carries the nuances in a starred footnote: the Send Feedback form in the app's Settings only sends feedback when the user deliberately opens it and sends, never automatically (see §13.6), and Ask plus long rewrites use Apple's Private Cloud Compute, which is end-to-end encrypted and keeps nothing (§13.1). It adds that Full Access only enables the keyboard's microphone so speech becomes text in real time (see §13.3), and that all of this can be verified in Apple's App Privacy Report.
